APT19.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Regsvr32
APT19.Description: APT19 used Regsvr32 to bypass application control techniques.[1]

APT19.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
APT19.Description: APT19 configured its payload to inject into the rundll32.exe.[1]

APT19.name: System Information Discovery
APT19.Description: APT19 collected system architecture information. APT19 used an HTTP malware variant and a Port 22 malware variant to gather the hostname and CPU information from the victim’s machine.[1][4]

APT19.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
APT19.Description: APT19 used an HTTP malware variant and a Port 22 malware variant to collect the MAC address and IP address from the victim’s machine.[4]

APT19.name: System Owner/User Discovery
APT19.Description: APT19 used an HTTP malware variant and a Port 22 malware variant to collect the victim’s username.[4]

APT19.name: User Execution: Malicious File
APT19.Description: APT19 attempted to get users to launch malicious attachments delivered via spearphishing emails.[1]

APT28.name: Access Token Manipulation: Token Impersonation/Theft
APT28.Description: APT28 has used CVE-2015-1701 to access the SYSTEM token and copy it into the current process as part of privilege escalation.[25]

APT28.name: Account Manipulation: Additional Email Delegate Permissions
APT28.Description: APT28 has used a Powershell cmdlet to grant the ApplicationImpersonation role to a compromised account.[2]

APT28.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Domains
APT28.Description: APT28 registered domains imitating NATO, OSCE security websites, Caucasus information resources, and other organizations.[6][14][26]

APT28.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Web Services
APT28.Description: APT28 has used newly-created Blogspot pages for credential harvesting operations.[26]

APT28.name: Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning
APT28.Description: APT28 has performed large-scale scans in an attempt to find vulnerable servers.[27]

APT28.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
APT28.Description: Later implants used by APT28, such as CHOPSTICK, use a blend of HTTP, HTTPS, and other legitimate channels for C2, depending on module configuration.[6][2]

APT28.name: Application Layer Protocol: Mail Protocols
APT28.Description: APT28 has used IMAP, POP3, and SMTP for a communication channel in various implants, including using self-registered Google Mail accounts and later compromised email servers of its victims.[6][2]

APT28.name: Archive Collected Data
APT28.Description: APT28 used a publicly available tool to gather and compress multiple documents on the DCCC and DNC networks.[3]

APT28.name: Archive via Utility
APT28.Description: APT28 has used a variety of utilities, including WinRAR, to archive collected data with password protection.[2]

APT28.name: Automated Collection
APT28.Description: APT28 used a publicly available tool to gather and compress multiple documents on the DCCC and DNC networks.[3]

APT28.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
APT28.Description: APT28 has deployed malware that has copied itself to the startup directory for persistence.[21]

APT28.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Logon Script (Windows)
APT28.Description: An APT28 loader Trojan adds the Registry key HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript to establish persistence.[28]

APT28.name: Brute Force
APT28.Description: APT28 can perform brute force attacks to obtain credentials.[27][21][29]

APT28.name: Password Guessing
APT28.Description: APT28 has used a brute-force/password-spray tooling that operated in two modes: in brute-force mode it typically sent over 300 authentication attempts per hour per targeted account over the course of several hours or days.[24] APT28 has also used a Kubernetes cluster to conduct distributed, large-scale password guessing attacks.[2]

APT28.name: Password Spraying
APT28.Description: APT28 has used a brute-force/password-spray tooling that operated in two modes: in password-spraying mode it conducted approximately four authentication attempts per hour per targeted account over the course of several days or weeks.[24][29] APT28 has also used a Kubernetes cluster to conduct distributed, large-scale password spray attacks.[2]

APT28.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
APT28.Description: APT28 downloads and executes PowerShell scripts and performs PowerShell commands.[11][21][2]

APT28.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
APT28.Description: An APT28 loader Trojan uses a cmd.exe and batch script to run its payload.[28] The group has also used macros to execute payloads.[18][30][17][21]

APT28.name: Communication Through Removable Media
APT28.Description: APT28 uses a tool that captures information from air-gapped computers via an infected USB and transfers it to network-connected computer when the USB is inserted.[31]

APT28.name: Compromise Accounts: Email Accounts
APT28.Description: APT28 has used compromised email accounts to send credential phishing emails.[26]

APT28.name: Data from Information Repositories
APT28.Description: APT28 has collected files from various information repositories.[2]

APT28.name: Sharepoint
APT28.Description: APT28 has collected information from Microsoft SharePoint services within target networks.[32]

APT28.name: Data from Local System
APT28.Description: APT28 has retrieved internal documents from machines inside victim environments, including by using Forfiles to stage documents before exfiltration.[33][3][27][2]

APT28.name: Data from Network Shared Drive
APT28.Description: APT28 has collected files from network shared drives.[2]

APT28.name: Data from Removable Media
APT28.Description: An APT28 backdoor may collect the entire contents of an inserted USB device.[31]

APT28.name: Data Obfuscation: Junk Data
APT28.Description: APT28 added "junk data" to each encoded string, preventing trivial decoding without knowledge of the junk removal algorithm. Each implant was given a "junk length" value when created, tracked by the controller software to allow seamless communication but prevent analysis of the command protocol on the wire.[6]

APT28.name: Data Staged: Local Data Staging
APT28.Description: APT28 has stored captured credential information in a file named pi.log.[31]

APT28.name: Data Staged: Remote Data Staging
APT28.Description: APT28 has staged archives of collected data on a target's Outlook Web Access (OWA) server.[2]

APT28.name: Data Transfer Size Limits
APT28.Description: APT28 has split archived exfiltration files into chunks smaller than 1MB.[2]

APT28.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
APT28.Description: An APT28 macro uses the command certutil -decode to decode contents of a .txt file storing the base64 encoded payload.[34][11]

APT28.name: Drive-by Compromise
APT28.Description: APT28 has compromised targets via strategic web compromise utilizing custom exploit kits.[16]

APT28.name: Email Collection: Remote Email Collection
APT28.Description: APT28 has collected emails from victim Microsoft Exchange servers.[3][2]

APT28.name: Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography
APT28.Description: APT28 installed a Delphi backdoor that used a custom algorithm for C2 communications.[13]

APT28.name: Event Triggered Execution: Component Object Model Hijacking
APT28.Description: APT28 has used COM hijacking for persistence by replacing the legitimate MMDeviceEnumerator object with a payload.[35][13]

APT28.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
APT28.Description: APT28 has exfiltrated archives of collected data previously staged on a target's OWA server via HTTPS.[2]

APT28.name: Exfiltration Over Web Service
APT28.Description: APT28 can exfiltrate data over Google Drive.[21]

APT28.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
APT28.Description: APT28 has used a variety of public exploits, including CVE 2020-0688 and CVE 2020-17144, to gain execution on vulnerable Microsoft Exchange; they have also conducted SQL injection attacks against external websites.[14][2]

APT28.name: Exploitation for Client Execution
APT28.Description: APT28 has exploited Microsoft Office vulnerability CVE-2017-0262 for execution.[22]

APT28.name: Exploitation for Defense Evasion
APT28.Description: APT28 has used CVE-2015-4902 to bypass security features.[36][31]

APT28.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
APT28.Description: APT28 has exploited CVE-2014-4076, CVE-2015-2387, CVE-2015-1701, CVE-2017-0263 to escalate privileges.[36][31][22]

APT28.name: Exploitation of Remote Services
APT28.Description: APT28 exploited a Windows SMB Remote Code Execution Vulnerability to conduct lateral movement.[6][37][38]

APT28.name: External Remote Services
APT28.Description: APT28 has used Tor and a variety of commercial VPN services to route brute force authentication attempts.[2]

APT28.name: File and Directory Discovery
APT28.Description: APT28 has used Forfiles to locate PDF, Excel, and Word documents during collection. The group also searched a compromised DCCC computer for specific terms.[33][3]

APT28.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
APT28.Description: APT28 has harvested user's login credentials.[29]

APT28.name: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Files and Directories
APT28.Description: APT28 has saved files with hidden file attributes.[18][18]

APT28.name: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Window
APT28.Description: APT28 has used the WindowStyle parameter to conceal PowerShell windows.[11] [39]

APT28.name: Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs
APT28.Description: APT28 has cleared event logs, including by using the commands wevtutil cl System and wevtutil cl Security.[5][3]

APT28.name: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
APT28.Description: APT28 has intentionally deleted computer files to cover their tracks, including with use of the program CCleaner.[3]

APT28.name: Indicator Removal: Timestomp
APT28.Description: APT28 has performed timestomping on victim files.[5]

APT28.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
APT28.Description: APT28 has downloaded additional files, including by using a first-stage downloader to contact the C2 server to obtain the second-stage implant.[36][28][17][21][2]

APT28.name: Input Capture: Keylogging
APT28.Description: APT28 has used tools to perform keylogging.[31][3][21]

APT28.name: Inter-Process Communication: Dynamic Data Exchange
APT28.Description: APT28 has delivered JHUHUGIT and Koadic by executing PowerShell commands through DDE in Word documents.[39][40][11]

APT28.name: Masquerading
APT28.Description: APT28 has renamed the WinRAR utility to avoid detection.[2]

APT28.name: Match Legitimate Name or Location
APT28.Description: APT28 has changed extensions on files containing exfiltrated data to make them appear benign, and renamed a web shell instance to appear as a legitimate OWA page.[2]

APT28.name: Network Denial of Service
APT28.Description: In 2016, APT28 conducted a distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack against the World Anti-Doping Agency.[14]

APT28.name: Network Sniffing
APT28.Description: APT28 deployed the open source tool Responder to conduct NetBIOS Name Service poisoning, which captured usernames and hashed passwords that allowed access to legitimate credentials.[6][37] APT28 close-access teams have used Wi-Fi pineapples to intercept Wi-Fi signals and user credentials.[14]

APT28.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
APT28.Description: APT28 encrypted a .dll payload using RTL and a custom encryption algorithm. APT28 has also obfuscated payloads with base64, XOR, and RC4.[36][34][11][18][17]

APT28.name: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
APT28.Description: APT28 has obtained and used open-source tools like Koadic, Mimikatz, and Responder.[11][22][37]

APT28.name: Office Application Startup: Office Test
APT28.Description: APT28 has used the Office Test persistence mechanism within Microsoft Office by adding the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office test\Special\Perf to execute code.[41]

APT28.name: OS Credential Dumping
APT28.Description: APT28 regularly deploys both publicly available (ex: Mimikatz) and custom password retrieval tools on victims.[42][3][14]

APT28.name: LSASS Memory
APT28.Description: APT28 regularly deploys both publicly available (ex: Mimikatz) and custom password retrieval tools on victims.[42][3] They have also dumped the LSASS process memory using the MiniDump function.[2]

APT28.name: NTDS
APT28.Description: APT28 has used the ntdsutil.exe utility to export the Active Directory database for credential access.[2]

APT28.name: Peripheral Device Discovery
APT28.Description: APT28 uses a module to receive a notification every time a USB mass storage device is inserted into a victim.[31]

APT28.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
APT28.Description: APT28 sent spearphishing emails containing malicious Microsoft Office and RAR attachments.[34][10][11][3][22][17][21][16]

APT28.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
APT28.Description: APT28 sent spearphishing emails which used a URL-shortener service to masquerade as a legitimate service and to redirect targets to credential harvesting sites.[3][13][14][16]

APT28.name: Phishing for Information
APT28.Description: APT28 has used spearphishing to compromise credentials.[29][16]

APT28.name: Spearphishing Link
APT28.Description: APT28 has conducted credential phishing campaigns with embedded links to attacker-controlled domains.[26]

APT28.name: Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit
APT28.Description: APT28 has deployed a bootkit along with Downdelph to ensure its persistence on the victim. The bootkit shares code with some variants of BlackEnergy.[20]

APT28.name: Process Discovery
APT28.Description: An APT28 loader Trojan will enumerate the victim's processes searching for explorer.exe if its current process does not have necessary permissions.[28]

APT28.name: Proxy: External Proxy
APT28.Description: APT28 used other victims as proxies to relay command traffic, for instance using a compromised Georgian military email server as a hop point to NATO victims. The group has also used a tool that acts as a proxy to allow C2 even if the victim is behind a router. APT28 has also used a machine to relay and obscure communications between CHOPSTICK and their server.[6][36][3]

APT28.name: Proxy: Multi-hop Proxy
APT28.Description: APT28 has routed traffic over Tor and VPN servers to obfuscate their activities.[21]

APT28.name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
APT28.Description: APT28 has mapped network drives using Net and administrator credentials.[2]

APT28.name: Replication Through Removable Media
APT28.Description: APT28 uses a tool to infect connected USB devices and transmit itself to air-gapped computers when the infected USB device is inserted.[31]

APT28.name: Rootkit
APT28.Description: APT28 has used a UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) rootkit known as LoJax.[12][43]

APT28.name: Screen Capture
APT28.Description: APT28 has used tools to take screenshots from victims.[42][44][3][16]

APT28.name: Server Software Component: Web Shell
APT28.Description: APT28 has used a modified and obfuscated version of the reGeorg web shell to maintain persistence on a target's Outlook Web Access (OWA) server.[2]

APT28.name: Steal Application Access Token
APT28.Description: APT28 has used several malicious applications to steal user OAuth access tokens including applications masquerading as "Google Defender" "Google Email Protection," and "Google Scanner" for Gmail users. They also targeted Yahoo users with applications masquerading as "Delivery Service" and "McAfee Email Protection".[45]

APT28.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
APT28.Description: APT28 executed CHOPSTICK by using rundll32 commands such as rundll32.exe "C:\Windows\twain_64.dll". APT28 also executed a .dll for a first stage dropper using rundll32.exe. An APT28 loader Trojan saved a batch script that uses rundll32 to execute a DLL payload.[5][36][11][28][13][2]

APT28.name: Template Injection
APT28.Description: APT28 used weaponized Microsoft Word documents abusing the remote template function to retrieve a malicious macro. [46]

APT28.name: Trusted Relationship
APT28.Description: Once APT28 gained access to the DCCC network, the group then proceeded to use that access to compromise the DNC network.[3]

APT28.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token
APT28.Description: APT28 has used several malicious applications that abused OAuth access tokens to gain access to target email accounts, including Gmail and Yahoo Mail.[45]

APT28.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
APT28.Description: APT28 has used pass the hash for lateral movement.[31]

APT28.name: User Execution: Malicious Link
APT28.Description: APT28 has tricked unwitting recipients into clicking on malicious hyperlinks within emails crafted to resemble trustworthy senders.[14][16]

APT28.name: User Execution: Malicious File
APT28.Description: APT28 attempted to get users to click on Microsoft Office attachments containing malicious macro scripts.[34][17][16]

APT28.name: Valid Accounts
APT28.Description: APT28 has used legitimate credentials to gain initial access, maintain access, and exfiltrate data from a victim network. The group has specifically used credentials stolen through a spearphishing email to login to the DCCC network. The group has also leveraged default manufacturer's passwords to gain initial access to corporate networks via IoT devices such as a VOIP phone, printer, and video decoder.[47][3][23][2]

APT28.name: Cloud Accounts
APT28.Description: APT28 has used compromised Office 365 service accounts with Global Administrator privileges to collect email from user inboxes.[2]

APT28.name: Web Service: Bidirectional Communication
APT28.Description: APT28 has used Google Drive for C2.[21]

APT29.name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Bypass User Account Control
APT29.Description: APT29 has bypassed UAC.[24]

APT29.name: Account Discovery
APT29.Description: APT29 obtained a list of users and their roles from an Exchange server using Get-ManagementRoleAssignment.[12]

APT29.name: Domain Account
APT29.Description: APT29 has used PowerShell to discover domain accounts by executing Get-ADUser and Get-ADGroupMember.[17][14]

APT29.name: Cloud Account
APT29.Description: APT29 has conducted enumeration of Azure AD accounts.[25]

APT29.name: Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials
APT29.Description: APT29 has added credentials to OAuth Applications and Service Principals.[26][17]

APT29.name: Account Manipulation: Additional Email Delegate Permissions
APT29.Description: APT29 added their own devices as allowed IDs for active sync using Set-CASMailbox, allowing it to obtain copies of victim mailboxes. It also added additional permissions (such as Mail.Read and Mail.ReadWrite) to compromised Application or Service Principals.[12][26][25]

APT29.name: Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Roles
APT29.Description: APT29 has granted company administrator privileges to a newly created service principal.[17]

APT29.name: Account Manipulation: Device Registration
APT29.Description: APT29 registered devices in order to enable mailbox syncing via the Set-CASMailbox command.[12]

APT29.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Domains
APT29.Description: APT29 has acquired C2 domains, sometimes through resellers.[10][27][18]

APT29.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Web Services
APT29.Description: APT29 has registered algorithmically generated Twitter handles that are used for C2 by malware, such as HAMMERTOSS. APT29 has also used legitimate web services such as Dropbox and Constant Contact in their operations.[28][18]

APT29.name: Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning
APT29.Description: APT29 has conducted widespread scanning of target environments to identify vulnerabilities for exploit.[13]

APT29.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
APT29.Description: APT29 has used HTTP for C2 and data exfiltration.[12]

APT29.name: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility
APT29.Description: APT29 used 7-Zip to compress stolen emails into password-protected archives prior to exfiltration; APT29 has also compressed text files into zipped archives.[12][29][17]

APT29.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
APT29.Description: APT29 added Registry Run keys to establish persistence.[24]

APT29.name: Brute Force: Password Spraying
APT29.Description: APT29 has conducted brute force password spray attacks.[20][25]

APT29.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
APT29.Description: APT29 has used encoded PowerShell scripts uploaded to CozyCar installations to download and install SeaDuke. APT29 also used PowerShell to create new tasks on remote machines, identify configuration settings, evade defenses, exfiltrate data, and to execute other commands.[12][30][31][24][32][17][33][15]

APT29.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
APT29.Description: APT29 used cmd.exe to execute commands on remote machines.[12][30]

APT29.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
APT29.Description: APT29 has written malware variants in Visual Basic.[13]

APT29.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python
APT29.Description: APT29 has developed malware variants written in Python.[22]

APT29.name: Compromise Accounts: Email Accounts
APT29.Description: APT29 has compromised email accounts to further enable phishing campaigns.[34]

APT29.name: Compromise Infrastructure: Domains
APT29.Description: APT29 has compromised domains to use for C2.[10]

APT29.name: Create Account: Cloud Account
APT29.Description: APT29 can create new users through Azure AD.[25]

APT29.name: Credentials from Password Stores
APT29.Description: APT29 used account credentials they obtained to attempt access to Group Managed Service Account (gMSA) passwords.[29]

APT29.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
APT29.Description: APT29 has stolen user's saved passwords from Chrome.[17]

APT29.name: Data from Information Repositories
APT29.Description: APT29 has accessed victims’ internal knowledge repositories (wikis) to view sensitive corporate information on products, services, and internal business operations.[17]

APT29.name: Code Repositories
APT29.Description: APT29 has downloaded source code from code repositories.[35]

APT29.name: Data from Local System
APT29.Description: APT29 has extracted files from compromised networks.[12]

APT29.name: Data Obfuscation: Steganography
APT29.Description: APT29 has used steganography to hide C2 communications in images.[22]

APT29.name: Data Staged: Remote Data Staging
APT29.Description: APT29 staged data and files in password-protected archives on a victim's OWA server.[12]

APT29.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
APT29.Description: APT29 used 7-Zip to decode its Raindrop malware.[36]

APT29.name: Develop Capabilities: Malware
APT29.Description: APT29 has leveraged numerous pieces of malware that appear to be unique to APT29 and were likely developed for or by the group.[9][11][29]

APT29.name: Develop Capabilities: Digital Certificates
APT29.Description: APT29 has created self-signed digital certificates to enable mutual TLS authentication for malware.[37][38]

APT29.name: Domain Policy Modification: Domain Trust Modification
APT29.Description: APT29 changed domain federation trust settings using Azure AD administrative permissions to configure the domain to accept authorization tokens signed by their own SAML signing certificate.[39][14]

APT29.name: Domain Trust Discovery
APT29.Description: APT29 used the Get-AcceptedDomain PowerShell cmdlet to enumerate accepted domains through an Exchange Management Shell.[12] They also used AdFind to enumerate domains and to discover trust between federated domains.[29][17]

APT29.name: Dynamic Resolution
APT29.Description: APT29 used dynamic DNS resolution to construct and resolve to randomly-generated subdomains for C2.[12]

APT29.name: Email Collection: Remote Email Collection
APT29.Description: APT29 collected emails from specific individuals, such as executives and IT staff, using New-MailboxExportRequest followed by Get-MailboxExportRequest.[12][13]

APT29.name: Encrypted Channel
APT29.Description: APT29 has used multiple layers of encryption within malware to protect C2 communication.[15]

APT29.name: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription
APT29.Description: APT29 has used WMI event subscriptions for persistence.[24][22][39][29]

APT29.name: Event Triggered Execution: Accessibility Features
APT29.Description: APT29 used sticky-keys to obtain unauthenticated, privileged console access.[24][40]

APT29.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
APT29.Description: APT29 has exfiltrated collected data over a simple HTTPS request to a password-protected archive staged on a victim's OWA servers.[12]

APT29.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
APT29.Description: APT29 has exploited CVE-2019-19781 for Citrix, CVE-2019-11510 for Pulse Secure VPNs, CVE-2018-13379 for FortiGate VPNs, and CVE-2019-9670 in Zimbra software to gain access. They have also exploited CVE-2020-0688 against the Microsoft Exchange Control Panel to regain access to a network.[23][12][13]

APT29.name: Exploitation for Client Execution
APT29.Description: APT29 has used multiple software exploits for common client software, like Microsoft Word, Exchange, and Adobe Reader, to gain code execution.[3][13][18]

APT29.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
APT29.Description: APT29 has exploited CVE-2021-36934 to escalate privileges on a compromised host.[33]

APT29.name: External Remote Services
APT29.Description: APT29 has used compromised identities to access networks via SSH, VPNs, and other remote access tools.[10][23][17]

APT29.name: File and Directory Discovery
APT29.Description: APT29 obtained information about the configured Exchange virtual directory using Get-WebServicesVirtualDirectory.[12]

APT29.name: Forge Web Credentials: Web Cookies
APT29.Description: APT29 has bypassed MFA set on OWA accounts by generating a cookie value from a previously stolen secret key.[12]

APT29.name: Forge Web Credentials: SAML Tokens
APT29.Description: APT29 created tokens using compromised SAML signing certificates.[26][14]

APT29.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
APT29.Description: APT29 has conducted credential theft operations to obtain credentials to be used for access to victim environments.[17]

APT29.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
APT29.Description: APT29 used the service control manager on a remote system to disable services associated with security monitoring products.[29]

APT29.name: Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging
APT29.Description: APT29 used AUDITPOL to prevent the collection of audit logs.[29]

APT29.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall
APT29.Description: APT29 used netsh to configure firewall rules that limited certain UDP outbound packets.[29]

APT29.name: Indicator Removal
APT29.Description: APT29 temporarily replaced legitimate utilities with their own, executed their payload, and then restored the original file.[9]

APT29.name: File Deletion
APT29.Description: APT29 routinely removed their tools, including custom backdoors, once remote access was achieved. APT29 has also used SDelete to remove artifacts from victims.[9][24]

APT29.name: Timestomp
APT29.Description: APT29 modified timestamps of backdoors to match legitimate Windows files.[29]

APT29.name: Clear Mailbox Data
APT29.Description: APT29 removed evidence of email export requests using Remove-MailboxExportRequest.[12]

APT29.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
APT29.Description: APT29 has downloaded additional tools, such as TEARDROP malware and Cobalt Strike, to a compromised host following initial access.[9]

APT29.name: Masquerading
APT29.Description: APT29 has set the hostnames of its C2 infrastructure to match legitimate hostnames in the victim environment. They have also used IP addresses originating from the same country as the victim for their VPN infrastructure.[9]

APT29.name: Masquerade Task or Service
APT29.Description: APT29 named tasks \Microsoft\Windows\SoftwareProtectionPlatform\EventCacheManager in order to appear legitimate.[12]

APT29.name: Match Legitimate Name or Location
APT29.Description: APT29 renamed software and DLL's with legitimate names to appear benign.[12][30][16]

APT29.name: Modify Authentication Process: Hybrid Identity
APT29.Description: APT29 has edited the Microsoft.IdentityServer.Servicehost.exe.config file to load a malicious DLL into the AD FS process, thereby enabling persistent access to any service federated with AD FS for a user with a specified User Principal Name.[41]

APT29.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
APT29.Description: APT29 has used repeated MFA requests to gain access to victim accounts.[42]

APT29.name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
APT29.Description: APT29 has used TCP for C2 communications.[32]

APT29.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
APT29.Description: APT29 has used encoded PowerShell commands.[32]

APT29.name: Binary Padding
APT29.Description: APT29 has used large file sizes to avoid detection.[16]

APT29.name: Software Packing
APT29.Description: APT29 used UPX to pack files.[24]

APT29.name: HTML Smuggling
APT29.Description: APT29 has embedded an ISO file within an HTML attachment that contained JavaScript code to initiate malware execution.[33]

APT29.name: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
APT29.Description: APT29 has obtained and used a variety of tools including Mimikatz, SDelete, Tor, meek, and Cobalt Strike.[24][3][32]

APT29.name: OS Credential Dumping: DCSync
APT29.Description: APT29 leveraged privileged accounts to replicate directory service data with domain controllers.[39][29][17]

APT29.name: Permission Groups Discovery
APT29.Description: APT29 used the Get-ManagementRoleAssignment PowerShell cmdlet to enumerate Exchange management role assignments through an Exchange Management Shell.[12]

APT29.name: Domain Groups
APT29.Description: APT29 has used AdFind to enumerate domain groups.[17]

APT29.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
APT29.Description: APT29 has used spearphishing emails with an attachment to deliver files with exploits to initial victims.[3][32][22][18][33][15]

APT29.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
APT29.Description: APT29 has used spearphishing with a link to trick victims into clicking on a link to a zip file containing malicious files.[24][18][43]

APT29.name: Phishing: Spearphishing via Service
APT29.Description: APT29 has used the legitimate mailing service Constant Contact to send phishing e-mails.[13]

APT29.name: Process Discovery
APT29.Description: APT29 has used multiple command-line utilities to enumerate running processes.[12][29][17]

APT29.name: Proxy: Internal Proxy
APT29.Description: APT29 has used SSH port forwarding capabilities on public-facing systems, and configured at least one instance of Cobalt Strike to use a network pipe over SMB during the 2020 SolarWinds intrusion.[36][17]

APT29.name: Proxy: Multi-hop Proxy
APT29.Description: A backdoor used by APT29 created a Tor hidden service to forward traffic from the Tor client to local ports 3389 (RDP), 139 (Netbios), and 445 (SMB) enabling full remote access from outside the network and has also used TOR.[24][25]

APT29.name: Proxy: Domain Fronting
APT29.Description: APT29 has used the meek domain fronting plugin for Tor to hide the destination of C2 traffic.[24]

APT29.name: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
APT29.Description: APT29 has used RDP sessions from public-facing systems to internal servers.[17]

APT29.name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
APT29.Description: APT29 has used administrative accounts to connect over SMB to targeted users.[17]

APT29.name: Remote Services: Windows Remote Management
APT29.Description: APT29 has used WinRM via PowerShell to execute command and payloads on remote hosts.[36]

APT29.name: Remote System Discovery
APT29.Description: APT29 has used AdFind to enumerate remote systems.[29]

APT29.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
APT29.Description: APT29 used scheduler and schtasks to create new tasks on remote hosts as part of lateral movement.[12] They have manipulated scheduled tasks by updating an existing legitimate task to execute their tools and then returned the scheduled task to its original configuration.[9] APT29 also created a scheduled task to maintain SUNSPOT persistence when the host booted during the 2020 SolarWinds intrusion.[11] They previously used named and hijacked scheduled tasks to also establish persistence.[24]

APT29.name: Server Software Component: Web Shell
APT29.Description: APT29 has installed web shells on exploited Microsoft Exchange servers.[13]

APT29.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
APT29.Description: APT29 has abused misconfigured AD CS certificate templates to impersonate admin users and create additional authentication certificates.[44]

APT29.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
APT29.Description: APT29 obtained Ticket Granting Service (TGS) tickets for Active Directory Service Principle Names to crack offline.[29]

APT29.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
APT29.Description: APT29 has stolen Chrome browser cookies by copying the Chrome profile directories of targeted users.[17]

APT29.name: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing
APT29.Description: APT29 was able to get SUNBURST signed by SolarWinds code signing certificates by injecting the malware into the SolarWinds Orion software lifecycle.[9]

APT29.name: Subvert Trust Controls: Mark-of-the-Web Bypass
APT29.Description: APT29 has embedded ISO images and VHDX files in HTML to evade Mark-of-the-Web.[33]

APT29.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
APT29.Description: APT29 gained initial network access to some victims via a trojanized update of SolarWinds Orion software.[9][13][14][25]

APT29.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Mshta
APT29.Description: APT29 has use mshta to execute malicious scripts on a compromised host.[33]

APT29.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
APT29.Description: APT29 has used Rundll32.exe to execute payloads.[26][29][32]

APT29.name: System Information Discovery
APT29.Description: APT29 used fsutil to check available free space before executing actions that might create large files on disk.[29]

APT29.name: System Network Configuration Discovery: Internet Connection Discovery
APT29.Description: APT29 has used GoldFinder to perform HTTP GET requests to check internet connectivity and identify HTTP proxy servers and other redirectors that an HTTP request travels through.[10]

APT29.name: Trusted Relationship
APT29.Description: APT29 has gained access through compromised accounts at cloud solution partners, and used compromised certificates issued by Mimecast to authenticate to Mimecast customer systems.[13][17][25]

APT29.name: Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys
APT29.Description: APT29 obtained PKI keys, certificate files and the private encryption key from an Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) container to decrypt corresponding SAML signing certificates.[39][13]

APT29.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
APT29.Description: APT29 used forged SAML tokens that allowed the actors to impersonate users and bypass MFA, enabling APT29 to access enterprise cloud applications and services.[39][14]

APT29.name: Application Access Token
APT29.Description: APT29 has used compromised service principals to make changes to the Office 365 environment.[17]

APT29.name: Pass the Ticket
APT29.Description: APT29 used Kerberos ticket attacks for lateral movement.[24]

APT29.name: Web Session Cookie
APT29.Description: APT29 used stolen cookies to access cloud resources, and a forged duo-sid cookie to bypass MFA set on an email account.[12][17]

APT29.name: User Execution: Malicious Link
APT29.Description: APT29 has used various forms of spearphishing attempting to get a user to click on a malicous link.[32][22][18][43]

APT29.name: User Execution: Malicious File
APT29.Description: APT29 has used various forms of spearphishing attempting to get a user to open attachments, including, but not limited to, malicious Microsoft Word documents, .pdf, and .lnk files. [3] [32][22][33][15]

APT29.name: Valid Accounts
APT29.Description: APT29 used different compromised credentials for remote access and to move laterally.[9][10][13]

APT29.name: Domain Accounts
APT29.Description: APT29 has used valid accounts, including administrator accounts, to help facilitate lateral movement on compromised networks.[22][23][17]

APT29.name: Local Accounts
APT29.Description: APT29 has used compromised local accounts to access victims' networks.[17]

APT29.name: Cloud Accounts
APT29.Description: APT29 has used a compromised O365 administrator account to create a new Service Principal.[17]

APT29.name: Web Service: Bidirectional Communication
APT29.Description: APT29 has used social media platforms to hide communications to C2 servers.[22]

APT29.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
APT29.Description: APT29 used WMI to steal credentials and execute backdoors at a future time.[24] They have also used WMI for the remote execution of files for lateral movement.[39][29]

APT32.Description: APT32 ran legitimately-signed executables from Symantec and McAfee which load a malicious DLL. The group also side-loads its backdoor by dropping a library and a legitimate, signed executable (AcroTranscoder).[4][7][5]

APT32.name: Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs
APT32.Description: APT32 has cleared select event log entries.[1]

APT32.name: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
APT32.Description: APT32's macOS backdoor can receive a "delete" command.[9]

APT32.name: Indicator Removal: Timestomp
APT32.Description: APT32 has used scheduled task raw XML with a backdated timestamp of June 2, 2016. The group has also set the creation time of the files dropped by the second stage of the exploit to match the creation time of kernel32.dll. Additionally, APT32 has used a random value to modify the timestamp of the file storing the clientID.[1][5][9]

APT32.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
APT32.Description: APT32 has added JavaScript to victim websites to download additional frameworks that profile and compromise website visitors.[2]

APT32.name: Input Capture: Keylogging
APT32.Description: APT32 has abused the PasswordChangeNotify to monitor for and capture account password changes.[7]

APT32.name: Lateral Tool Transfer
APT32.Description: APT32 has deployed tools after moving laterally using administrative accounts.[7]

APT32.name: Masquerading
APT32.Description: APT32 has disguised a Cobalt Strike beacon as a Flash Installer.[7]

APT32.name: Rename System Utilities
APT32.Description: APT32 has moved and renamed pubprn.vbs to a .txt file to avoid detection.[10]

APT32.name: Masquerade Task or Service
APT32.Description: APT32 has used hidden or non-printing characters to help masquerade service names, such as appending a Unicode no-break space character to a legitimate service name. APT32 has also impersonated the legitimate Flash installer file name "install_flashplayer.exe".[1]

APT32.name: Match Legitimate Name or Location
APT32.Description: APT32 has renamed a NetCat binary to kb-10233.exe to masquerade as a Windows update. APT32 has also renamed a Cobalt Strike beacon payload to install_flashplayers.exe. [7][8]

APT32.name: Modify Registry
APT32.Description: APT32's backdoor has modified the Windows Registry to store the backdoor's configuration. [5]

APT32.name: Network Service Discovery
APT32.Description: APT32 performed network scanning on the network to search for open ports, services, OS finger-printing, and other vulnerabilities.[7]

APT32.name: Network Share Discovery
APT32.Description: APT32 used the net view command to show all shares available, including the administrative shares such as C$ and ADMIN$.[7]

APT32.name: Non-Standard Port
APT32.Description: An APT32 backdoor can use HTTP over a non-standard TCP port (e.g 14146) which is specified in the backdoor configuration.[5]

APT32.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
APT32.Description: APT32 uses the Invoke-Obfuscation framework to obfuscate their PowerShell and also performs other code obfuscation. APT32 has also encoded payloads using Base64 and a framework called "Dont-Kill-My-Cat (DKMC). APT32 also encrypts the library used for network exfiltration with AES-256 in CBC mode in their macOS backdoor.[1][11][3][4][7][5][9]

APT32.name: Binary Padding
APT32.Description: APT32 includes garbage code to mislead anti-malware software and researchers.[3][5]

APT32.name: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
APT32.Description: APT32 has obtained and used tools such as Mimikatz and Cobalt Strike, and a variety of other open-source tools from GitHub.[1][4]

APT32.name: Office Application Startup
APT32.Description: APT32 have replaced Microsoft Outlook's VbaProject.OTM file to install a backdoor macro for persistence.[4][7]

APT32.name: OS Credential Dumping
APT32.Description: APT32 used GetPassword_x64 to harvest credentials.[4][7]

APT32.name: LSASS Memory
APT32.Description: APT32 used Mimikatz and customized versions of Windows Credential Dumper to harvest credentials.[4][7]

APT32.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
APT32.Description: APT32 has sent spearphishing emails with a malicious executable disguised as a document or spreadsheet.[3][4][7][5][12][6]

APT32.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
APT32.Description: APT32 has sent spearphishing emails containing malicious links.[3][4][12][8][6]

APT32.name: Phishing for Information: Spearphishing Link
APT32.Description: APT32 has used malicious links to direct users to web pages designed to harvest credentials.[8]

APT32.name: Process Injection
APT32.Description: APT32 malware has injected a Cobalt Strike beacon into Rundll32.exe.[7]

APT32.name: Query Registry
APT32.Description: APT32's backdoor can query the Windows Registry to gather system information. [5]

APT32.name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
APT32.Description: APT32 used Net to use Windows' hidden network shares to copy their tools to remote machines for execution.[7]

APT32.name: Remote System Discovery
APT32.Description: APT32 has enumerated DC servers using the command net group "Domain Controllers" /domain. The group has also used the ping command.[7]

APT32.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
APT32.Description: APT32 has used scheduled tasks to persist on victim systems.[1][4][7][5]

APT32.name: Server Software Component: Web Shell
APT32.Description: APT32 has used Web shells to maintain access to victim websites.[2]

APT32.name: Software Deployment Tools
APT32.Description: APT32 compromised McAfee ePO to move laterally by distributing malware as a software deployment task.[1]

APT32.name: Stage Capabilities: Upload Malware
APT32.Description: APT32 has hosted malicious payloads in Dropbox, Amazon S3, and Google Drive for use during targeting.[8]

APT32.name: Stage Capabilities: Drive-by Target
APT32.Description: APT32 has stood up websites containing numerous articles and content scraped from the Internet to make them appear legitimate, but some of these pages include malicious JavaScript to profile the potential victim or infect them via a fake software update.[8]

APT32.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Mshta
APT32.Description: APT32 has used mshta.exe for code execution.[4][7]

APT32.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Regsvr32
APT32.Description: APT32 created a Scheduled Task/Job that used regsvr32.exe to execute a COM scriptlet that dynamically downloaded a backdoor and injected it into memory. The group has also used regsvr32 to run their backdoor.[5][1][7]

APT32.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
APT32.Description: APT32 malware has used rundll32.exe to execute an initial infection process.[7]

APT32.name: System Information Discovery
APT32.Description: APT32 has collected the OS version and computer name from victims. One of the group's backdoors can also query the Windows Registry to gather system information, and another macOS backdoor performs a fingerprint of the machine on its first connection to the C&C server. APT32 executed shellcode to identify the name of the infected host.[3][5][9][12]

APT32.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
APT32.Description: APT32 used the ipconfig /all command to gather the IP address from the system.[7]

APT32.name: System Network Connections Discovery
APT32.Description: APT32 used the netstat -anpo tcp command to display TCP connections on the victim's machine.[7]

APT32.name: System Owner/User Discovery
APT32.Description: APT32 collected the victim's username and executed the whoami command on the victim's machine. APT32 executed shellcode to collect the username on the victim's machine. [12][3][7]

APT32.name: System Script Proxy Execution: PubPrn
APT32.Description: APT32 has used PubPrn.vbs within execution scripts to execute malware, possibly bypassing defenses.[13]

APT32.name: System Services: Service Execution
APT32.Description: APT32's backdoor has used Windows services as a way to execute its malicious payload. [5]

APT32.name: Unsecured Credentials: Credentials in Registry
APT32.Description: APT32 used Outlook Credential Dumper to harvest credentials stored in Windows registry.[4][7]

APT32.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
APT32.Description: APT32 has used pass the hash for lateral movement.[7]

APT32.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
APT32.Description: APT32 successfully gained remote access by using pass the ticket.[7]

APT32.name: User Execution: Malicious Link
APT32.Description: APT32 has lured targets to download a Cobalt Strike beacon by including a malicious link within spearphishing emails.[7][8][6]

APT32.name: User Execution: Malicious File
APT32.Description: APT32 has attempted to lure users to execute a malicious dropper delivered via a spearphishing attachment.[3][4][5][12][6]

APT32.name: Valid Accounts: Local Accounts
APT32.Description: APT32 has used legitimate local admin account credentials.[1]

APT32.name: Web Service
APT32.Description: APT32 has used Dropbox, Amazon S3, and Google Drive to host malicious downloads.[8]

APT32.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
APT32.Description: APT32 used WMI to deploy their tools on remote machines and to gather information about the Outlook process.[7]

Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has used powershell.exe to download and execute scripts.[1][2][3][4][7][12]

Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has used a JavaScript backdoor that is capable of launching cmd.exe to execute shell commands.[11] The group has used an exploit toolkit known as Threadkit that launches .bat files.[1][2][4][11][13][12]

Cobalt Group.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has sent Word OLE compound documents with malicious obfuscated VBA macros that will run upon user execution.[1][2][4][11][13][12]

Cobalt Group.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has executed JavaScript scriptlets on the victim's machine.[1][2][4][11][13][12]

Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has created new services to establish persistence.[4]

Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has used the Plink utility to create SSH tunnels.[4]

Cobalt Group.name: Exploitation for Client Execution
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group had exploited multiple vulnerabilities for execution, including Microsoft’s Equation Editor (CVE-2017-11882), an Internet Explorer vulnerability (CVE-2018-8174), CVE-2017-8570, CVE-2017-0199, and CVE-2017-8759.[1][2][3][5][6][7][10][12]

Cobalt Group.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has used exploits to increase their levels of rights and privileges.[4]

Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group deleted the DLL dropper from the victim’s machine to cover their tracks.[1]

Cobalt Group.name: Inter-Process Communication: Dynamic Data Exchange
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has sent malicious Word OLE compound documents to victims.[1]

Cobalt Group.name: Network Service Discovery
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group leveraged an open-source tool called SoftPerfect Network Scanner to perform network scanning.[2][3][4]

Cobalt Group.name: Obfuscated Files or Information

Cobalt Group.name: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has obtained and used a variety of tools including Mimikatz, PsExec, Cobalt Strike, and SDelete.[3]

Cobalt Group.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has sent spearphishing emails with various attachment types to corporate and personal email accounts of victim organizations. Attachment types have included .rtf, .doc, .xls, archives containing LNK files, and password protected archives containing .exe and .scr executables.[1][2][3][4][5][6][13][12]

Cobalt Group.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has sent emails with URLs pointing to malicious documents.[1][9]

Cobalt Group.name: Process Injection
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has injected code into trusted processes.[4]

Cobalt Group.name: Protocol Tunneling
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has used the Plink utility to create SSH tunnels.[1][3][4]

Cobalt Group.name: Remote Access Software
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group used the Ammyy Admin tool as well as TeamViewer for remote access, including to preserve remote access if a Cobalt Strike module was lost.[2][3][4]

Cobalt Group.name: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has used Remote Desktop Protocol to conduct lateral movement.[4]

Cobalt Group.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has created Windows tasks to establish persistence.[4]

Cobalt Group.name: Software Discovery: Security Software Discovery
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group used a JavaScript backdoor that is capable of collecting a list of the security solutions installed on the victim's machine.[11]

Cobalt Group.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has compromised legitimate web browser updates to deliver a backdoor. [14]

Cobalt Group.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Odbcconf
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has used odbcconf to proxy the execution of malicious DLL files.[12]

Cobalt Group.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Regsvr32
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has used regsvr32.exe to execute scripts.[1][11][12]

Cobalt Group.name: User Execution: Malicious Link
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has sent emails containing malicious links that require users to execute a file or macro to infect the victim machine.[1][13][9]

Cobalt Group.name: User Execution: Malicious File
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group has sent emails containing malicious attachments that require users to execute a file or macro to infect the victim machine.[1][13]

Cobalt Group.name: XSL Script Processing
Cobalt Group.Description: Cobalt Group used msxsl.exe to bypass AppLocker and to invoke Jscript code from an XSL file.[1]

Dragonfly.Description: Dragonfly has compressed data into .zip files prior to exfiltration.[14]

Dragonfly.Description: Dragonfly has dropped and executed tools used for password cracking, including Hydra and CrackMapExec.[14][15]

Dragonfly.Description: Dragonfly has accessed email accounts using Outlook Web Access.[14]

Dragonfly.Description: Dragonfly has exploited CVE-2011-0611 in Adobe Flash Player to gain execution on a targeted system.[7]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has added accounts to specific groups with net localgroup.[11]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has registered domains to spoof targeted organizations and trusted third parties.[10][12][5][3][4][11]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has purchased hosting servers with virtual currency and prepaid cards.[11]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has hosted content used for targeting efforts via web services such as Blogspot.[13]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used modified versions of PHProxy to examine web traffic between the victim and the accessed website.[5]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used HTTP GET and POST requests for C2.[13]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used FTP to download additional malware to the target machine.[14]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used RC4 encryption before exfil.[15]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has placed scripts in the startup folder for persistence and modified the HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce Registry key.[15][5][16][13][11]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used Google Chrome browser extensions to infect victims and to steal passwords and cookies.[9][6]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has executed a variety of PowerShell scripts.[1][5][13][11]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has executed Windows commands by using cmd and running batch scripts.[13][11]

Kimsuky.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used Visual Basic to download malicious payloads.[10][14][16][13] Kimsuky has also used malicious VBA macros within maldocs disguised as forms that trigger when a victim types any content into the lure.[13]

Kimsuky.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used a macOS Python implant to gather data as well as MailFetcher.py code to automatically collect email data.[5][11]

Kimsuky.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used JScript for logging and downloading additional tools.[14][5]

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has compromised email accounts to send spearphishing e-mails.[14][4]

Kimsuky.name: Compromise Infrastructure: Domains
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has compromised legitimate sites and used them to distribute malware.[11]

Kimsuky.name: Create Account: Local Account
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has created accounts with net user.[11]

Kimsuky.name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has created new services for persistence.[15][5]

Kimsuky.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used browser extensions including Google Chrome to steal passwords and cookies from browsers. Kimsuky has also used Nirsoft's WebBrowserPassView tool to dump the passwords obtained from victims.[9][5][6][13]

Kimsuky.name: Data from Local System
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has collected Office, PDF, and HWP documents from its victims.[15][13]

Kimsuky.name: Data Staged: Local Data Staging
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has staged collected data files under C:\Program Files\Common Files\System\Ole DB\.[5][13]

Kimsuky.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has decoded malicious VBScripts using Base64.[13]

Kimsuky.name: Develop Capabilities
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky created and used a mailing toolkit to use in spearphishing attacks.[14]

Kimsuky.name: Malware
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has developed its own unique malware such as MailFetch.py for use in operations.[11][13]

Kimsuky.name: Email Collection: Remote Email Collection
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used tools such as the MailFetch mail crawler to collect victim emails (excluding spam) from online services via IMAP.[11]

Kimsuky.name: Email Collection: Email Forwarding Rule
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has set auto-forward rules on victim's e-mail accounts.[5]

Kimsuky.name: Establish Accounts: Social Media Accounts
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has created social media accounts to monitor news and security trends as well as potential targets.[11]

Kimsuky.name: Establish Accounts: Email Accounts
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has created email accounts for phishing operations.[11]

Kimsuky.name: Event Triggered Execution: Change Default File Association
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has a HWP document stealer module which changes the default program association in the registry to open HWP documents.[15]

Kimsuky.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has exfiltrated data over its C2 channel.[15][13]

Kimsuky.name: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has exfiltrated stolen files and data to actor-controlled Blogspot accounts.[13]

Kimsuky.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has exploited various vulnerabilities for initial access, including Microsoft Exchange vulnerability CVE-2020-0688.[11]

Kimsuky.name: External Remote Services
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used RDP to establish persistence.[5]

Kimsuky.name: File and Directory Discovery
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has the ability to enumerate all files and directories on an infected system.[15][13][11]

Kimsuky.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Employee Names
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has collected victim employee name information.[11]

Kimsuky.name: Gather Victim Org Information
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has collected victim organization information including but not limited to organization hierarchy, functions, press releases, and others.[11]

Kimsuky.name: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Users
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has run reg add ‘HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\SpecialAccounts\UserList’ /v to hide a newly created user.[11]

Kimsuky.name: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Window
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used an information gathering module that will hide an AV software window from the victim.[13]

Kimsuky.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has been observed turning off Windows Security Center and can hide the AV software window from the view of the infected user.[15][13]

Kimsuky.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has been observed disabling the system firewall.[15]

Kimsuky.name: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has deleted the exfiltrated data on disk after transmission. Kimsuky has also used an instrumentor script to terminate browser processes running on an infected system and then delete the cookie files on disk.[15][13][11]

Kimsuky.name: Indicator Removal: Timestomp
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has manipulated timestamps for creation or compilation dates to defeat anti-forensics.[3]

Kimsuky.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has downloaded additional scripts, tools, and malware onto victim systems.[16][13]

Kimsuky.name: Input Capture: Keylogging

Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has sent internal spearphishing emails for lateral movement after stealing victim information.[11]

Kimsuky.name: System Service Discovery
Kimsuky.Description: Kimsuky has used an instrumentor script to gather the names of all services running on a victim's system.[13]

LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has obtained passwords and session tokens with the use of the Redline password stealer.[2]

LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has searched a victim's network for organization collaboration channels like MS Teams or Slack to discover further high-privilege account credentials.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Sharepoint
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has searched a victim's network for collaboration platforms like SharePoint to discover further high-privilege account credentials.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Code Repositories
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has searched a victim's network for code repositories like GitLab and GitHub to discover further high-privilege account credentials.[2]

LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ uploaded sensitive files, information, and credentials from a targeted organization for extortion or public release.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Email Collection: Email Forwarding Rule
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has set an Office 365 tenant level mail transport rule to send all mail in and out of the targeted organization to the newly created account.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has exploited unpatched vulnerabilities on internally accessible servers including JIRA, GitLab, and Confluence for privilege escalation.[2]

LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has gained access to internet-facing systems and applications, including virtual private network (VPN), remote desktop protocol (RDP), and virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) including Citrix. [2]

LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has gathered detailed information of target employees to enhance their social engineering lures.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Email Addresses
