LAPSUS$.name: Gather Victim Org Information: Business Relationships
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has gathered detailed knowledge of an organization's supply chain relationships.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Roles
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has gathered detailed knowledge of team structures within a target organization.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Create Cloud Instance
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has created new virtual machines within the target's cloud environment after leveraging credential access to cloud assets.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Delete Cloud Instance
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has deleted the target's systems and resources in the cloud to trigger the organization's incident and crisis response process.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has replayed stolen session token and passwords to trigger simple-approval MFA prompts in hope of the legitimate user will grant necessary approval.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has spammed target users with MFA prompts in the hope that the legitimate user will grant necessary approval.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Obtain Capabilities: Malware
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ acquired and used the Redline password stealer in their operations.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has obtained tools such as AD Explorer inspection software for their operations.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: OS Credential Dumping: NTDS
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has used Windows built-in tool ntdsutil to extract the Active Directory (AD) database.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: OS Credential Dumping: DCSync
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has used DCSync attacks to gather credentials for privilege escalation routines.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Permission Groups Discovery: Domain Groups
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has used the AD Explorer tool to enumerate groups on a victim's network.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Proxy
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has leverage NordVPN for its egress points when targeting intended victims.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Search Closed Sources: Purchase Technical Data
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has purchased credentials and session tokens from criminal underground forums.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Search Open Websites/Domains: Code Repositories
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has searched public code repositories for exposed credentials.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Trusted Relationship
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has accessed internet-facing identity providers such as Azure Active Directory and Okta to target specific organizations.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: User Execution
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has recruited target organization employees or contractors who provide credentials and approve an associated MFA prompt, or install remote management software onto a corporate workstation, allowing LAPSUS$ to take control of an authenticated system.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Valid Accounts
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has used compromised credentials and/or session tokens to gain access into a victim's VPN, VDI, RDP, and IAMs.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Cloud Accounts
LAPSUS$.Description: LAPSUS$ has used compromised credentials to access cloud assets within a target organization.[2]

LAPSUS$.name: Mimikatz
LAPSUS$.Description: [2] Access Token Manipulation: SID-History Injection, Account Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Security Support Provider, Credentials from Password Stores, Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager, Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers, OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager, OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory, OS Credential Dumping: LSA Secrets, OS Credential Dumping: DCSync, Rogue Domain Controller, Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates, Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Silver Ticket, Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket, Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys, Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket, Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash

Lazarus Group.name: Access Token Manipulation: Create Process with Token
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group keylogger KiloAlfa obtains user tokens from interactive sessions to execute itself with API call CreateProcessAsUserA under that user's context.[3][8]

Lazarus Group.name: Account Discovery: Domain Account
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has queried an active directory server to obtain the list of accounts, including administrator accounts.[9]

Lazarus Group.name: Account Manipulation
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware WhiskeyDelta-Two contains a function that attempts to rename the administrator’s account.[3][10]

Lazarus Group.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Domains
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has acquired domains related to their campaigns to act as distribution points and C2 channels.[11][9][12]

Lazarus Group.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Server
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has acquired servers to host their malicious tools.[9]

Lazarus Group.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Web Services
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has hosted malicious downloads on Github and Dropbox.[11][13]

Lazarus Group.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group executed Responder using the command [Responder file path] -i [IP address] -rPv on a compromised host to harvest credentials and move laterally.[14]

Lazarus Group.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has conducted C2 over HTTP and HTTPS.[15][16][17][18][19][20][21]

Lazarus Group.name: Application Window Discovery
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia obtains and sends to its C2 server the title of the window for each running process. The KilaAlfa keylogger also reports the title of the window in the foreground.[3][22][8]

Lazarus Group.name: Archive Collected Data
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has compressed exfiltrated data with RAR and used RomeoDelta malware to archive specified directories in .zip format, encrypt the .zip file, and upload it to C2. [22][23][15][9]

Lazarus Group.name: Archive via Library
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia saves information gathered about the victim to a file that is compressed with Zlib, encrypted, and uploaded to a C2 server.[23][15]

Lazarus Group.name: Archive via Custom Method
Lazarus Group.Description: A Lazarus Group malware sample encrypts data using a simple byte based XOR operation prior to exfiltration.[3][22][23][15]

Lazarus Group.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has maintained persistence by loading malicious code into a startup folder or by adding a Registry Run key.[3][23][15][18][19]

Lazarus Group.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Shortcut Modification
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware has maintained persistence on a system by creating a LNK shortcut in the user’s Startup folder.[15][13]

Lazarus Group.name: Brute Force
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has performed brute force attacks against administrator accounts.[9]

Lazarus Group.name: Password Spraying
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware attempts to connect to Windows shares for lateral movement by using a generated list of usernames, which center around permutations of the username Administrator, and weak passwords.[3][23]

Lazarus Group.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used PowerShell to execute commands and malicious code.[9][12]

Lazarus Group.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware uses cmd.exe to execute commands on a compromised host.[3][10][15][24][20] A Destover-like variant used by Lazarus Group uses a batch file mechanism to delete its binaries from the system.[25]

Lazarus Group.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used VBA and embedded macros in Word documents to execute malicious code.[18][13][19][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Compromise Infrastructure: Domains
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has compromised legitimate domains, including those hosted in the US and Italy, for C2.[26]

Lazarus Group.name: Compromise Infrastructure: Server
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has compromised servers to stage malicious tools.[14][13][9][18]

Lazarus Group.name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
Lazarus Group.Description: Several Lazarus Group malware families install themselves as new services.[3][10]

Lazarus Group.name: Data Destruction
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used a custom secure delete function to overwrite file contents with data from heap memory.[3]

Lazarus Group.name: Data Encoding: Standard Encoding
Lazarus Group.Description: A Lazarus Group malware sample encodes data with base64.[15]

Lazarus Group.name: Data from Local System
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has collected data and files from compromised networks.[3][22][23][14][13][18]

Lazarus Group.name: Data Obfuscation: Protocol Impersonation
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware also uses a unique form of communication encryption known as FakeTLS that mimics TLS but uses a different encryption method, potentially evading SSL traffic inspection/decryption.[3][10][15][25]

Lazarus Group.name: Data Staged: Local Data Staging
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia saves information gathered about the victim to a file that is saved in the %TEMP% directory, then compressed, encrypted, and uploaded to a C2 server.[3][22]

Lazarus Group.name: Defacement: Internal Defacement
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group replaced the background wallpaper of systems with a threatening image after rendering the system unbootable with a Disk Structure Wipe.[10]

Lazarus Group.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used shellcode within macros to decrypt and manually map DLLs and shellcode into memory at runtime.[19][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Develop Capabilities: Malware
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has developed custom malware for use in their operations.[11][9][12][13]

Lazarus Group.name: Disk Wipe: Disk Content Wipe
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used malware like WhiskeyAlfa to overwrite the first 64MB of every drive with a mix of static and random buffers. A similar process is then used to wipe content in logical drives and, finally, attempt to wipe every byte of every sector on every drive. WhiskeyBravo can be used to overwrite the first 4.9MB of physical drives. WhiskeyDelta can overwrite the first 132MB or 1.5MB of each drive with random data from heap memory.[10]

Lazarus Group.name: Disk Wipe: Disk Structure Wipe
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware SHARPKNOT overwrites and deletes the Master Boot Record (MBR) on the victim's machine and has possessed MBR wiper malware since at least 2009.[24][3]

Lazarus Group.name: Drive-by Compromise
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group delivered RATANKBA and other malicious code to victims via a compromised legitimate website.[27][12]

Lazarus Group.name: Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography
Lazarus Group.Description: Several Lazarus Group malware families encrypt C2 traffic using custom code that uses XOR with an ADD operation and XOR with a SUB operation. Another Lazarus Group malware sample XORs C2 traffic. Other Lazarus Group malware uses Caracachs encryption to encrypt C2 payloads. Lazarus Group has also used AES to encrypt C2 traffic.[3][10][15][25][18]

Lazarus Group.name: Establish Accounts: Social Media Accounts
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has created new LinkedIn and Twitter accounts to conduct social engineering against potential victims.[13][9][12]

Lazarus Group.name: Establish Accounts: Email Accounts
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has created new email accounts for spearphishing operations.[9][14]

Lazarus Group.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware SierraBravo-Two generates an email message via SMTP containing information about newly infected victims.[3][23]

Lazarus Group.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has exfiltrated data and files over a C2 channel through its various tools and malware.[3][22][15][26]

Lazarus Group.name: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has exfiltrated stolen data to Dropbox using a customized version of dbxcli.[9][13]

Lazarus Group.name: Exploitation for Client Execution
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has exploited Adobe Flash vulnerability CVE-2018-4878 for execution.[28]

Lazarus Group.name: Fallback Channels
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware SierraAlfa sends data to one of the hard-coded C2 servers chosen at random, and if the transmission fails, chooses a new C2 server to attempt the transmission again.[3][23]

Lazarus Group.name: File and Directory Discovery
Lazarus Group.Description: Several Lazarus Group has conducted word searches on compromised machines to identify specific documents of interest. Lazarus Group malware can use a common function to identify target files by their extension, and some also enumerate files and directories, including a Destover-like variant that lists files and gathers information for all drives.[3][25][13][19][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group collected email addresses belonging to various departments of a targeted organization which were used in follow-on phishing campaigns.[14]

Lazarus Group.name: Gather Victim Org Information
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has studied publicly available information about a targeted organization to tailor spearphishing efforts against specific departments and/or individuals.[9][13][14]

Lazarus Group.name: Identify Roles
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has targeted specific individuals within an organization with tailored job vacancy announcements.[9][13]

Lazarus Group.name: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Files and Directories
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used a VBA Macro to set its file attributes to System and Hidden and has named files with a dot prefix to hide them from the Finder application.[15][16][17][19]

Lazarus Group.name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has replaced win_fw.dll, an internal component that is executed during IDA Pro installation, with a malicious DLL to download and execute a payload.[21]

Lazarus Group.name: Hijack Execution Flow: KernelCallbackTable
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has abused the KernelCallbackTable to hijack process control flow and execute shellcode.[19][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware TangoDelta attempts to terminate various processes associated with McAfee. Additionally, Lazarus Group malware SHARPKNOT disables the Microsoft Windows System Event Notification and Alerter services.[3][22][8][24].

Lazarus Group.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall
Lazarus Group.Description: Various Lazarus Group malware modifies the Windows firewall to allow incoming connections or disable it entirely using netsh. [3][22][8]

Lazarus Group.name: Indicator Removal
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has restored malicious KernelCallbackTable code to its original state after the process execution flow has been hijacked.[19]

Lazarus Group.name: Clear Command History
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has routinely deleted log files on a compromised router, including automatic log deletion through the use of the logrotate utility.[14]

Lazarus Group.name: File Deletion
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware has deleted files in various ways, including "suicide scripts" to delete malware binaries from the victim. Lazarus Group also uses secure file deletion to delete files from the victim.[3][25]

Lazarus Group.name: Timestomp
Lazarus Group.Description: Several Lazarus Group malware families use timestomping, including modifying the last write timestamp of a specified Registry key to a random date, as well as copying the timestamp for legitimate .exe files (such as calc.exe or mspaint.exe) to its dropped files.[3][10][22][25]

Lazarus Group.name: Indirect Command Execution
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group persistence mechanisms have used forfiles.exe to execute .htm files.[20]

Lazarus Group.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has downloaded files, malware, and tools from its C2 onto a compromised host.[3][10][22][16][17][13][14][18][9][12][19][20][21]

Lazarus Group.name: Input Capture: Keylogging
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware KiloAlfa contains keylogging functionality.[3][8]

Lazarus Group.name: Internal Spearphishing
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has conducted internal spearphishing from within a compromised organization.[13]

Lazarus Group.name: Masquerading
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has disguised malicious template files as JPEG files to avoid detection.[18]

Lazarus Group.name: Rename System Utilities
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has renamed system utilities such as wscript.exe and mshta.exe.[20]

Lazarus Group.name: Masquerade Task or Service
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used a scheduled task named SRCheck to mask the execution of a malicious .dll.[21]

Lazarus Group.name: Match Legitimate Name or Location
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has renamed malicious code to disguise it as Microsoft's narrator and other legitimate files.[29][9][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Multi-Stage Channels
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used multi-stage malware components that inject later stages into separate processes.[19]

Lazarus Group.name: Native API
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used the Windows API ObtainUserAgentString to obtain the User-Agent from a compromised host to connect to a C2 server.[18] Lazarus Group has also used various, often lesser known, functions to perform various types of Discovery and Process Injection.[19][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Network Service Discovery
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used nmap from a router VM to scan ports on systems within the restricted segment of an enterprise network.[14]

Lazarus Group.name: Non-Standard Port
Lazarus Group.Description: Some Lazarus Group malware uses a list of ordered port numbers to choose a port for C2 traffic, creating port-protocol mismatches.[3][23]

Lazarus Group.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used multiple types of encryption and encoding for their payloads, including AES, Caracachs, RC4, XOR, Base64, and other tricks such as creating aliases in code for Native API function names.[3][22][23][15][17][9][18][26][13][19][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Software Packing
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used Themida to pack malicious DLLs and other files.[13][26]

Lazarus Group.name: Dynamic API Resolution
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used a custom hashing method to resolve APIs used in shellcode.[19]

Lazarus Group.name: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has obtained a variety of tools for their operations, including Responder, PuTTy PSCP, Wake-On-Lan, ChromePass, and dbxcli.[9][13][14]

Lazarus Group.name: Obtain Capabilities: Code Signing Certificates
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used code signing certificates issued by Sectigo RSA for some of its malware and tools.[9]

Lazarus Group.name: Obtain Capabilities: Digital Certificates
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has obtained SSL certificates for their C2 domains.[11]

Lazarus Group.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has targeted victims with spearphishing emails containing malicious Microsoft Word documents.[28][14][18][19][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has sent malicious links to victims via email.[14][13][9]

Lazarus Group.name: Phishing: Spearphishing via Service
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used social media platforms, including LinkedIn and Twitter, to send spearphishing messages.[12][13][9]

Lazarus Group.name: Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware WhiskeyAlfa-Three modifies sector 0 of the Master Boot Record (MBR) to ensure that the malware will persist even if a victim machine shuts down.[3][10]

Lazarus Group.name: Process Discovery
Lazarus Group.Description: Several Lazarus Group malware families gather a list of running processes on a victim system and send it to their C2 server. A Destover-like variant used by Lazarus Group also gathers process times.[3][22][15][25][17][19]

Lazarus Group.name: Process Injection: Dynamic-link Library Injection
Lazarus Group.Description: A Lazarus Group malware sample performs reflective DLL injection.[15][19]

Lazarus Group.name: Proxy: Internal Proxy
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used a compromised router to serve as a proxy between a victim network's corporate and restricted segments.[14]

Lazarus Group.name: Proxy: External Proxy
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used multiple proxies to obfuscate network traffic from victims.[30][17]

Lazarus Group.name: Query Registry
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia checks Registry keys within HKCU and HKLM to determine if certain applications are present, including SecureCRT, Terminal Services, RealVNC, TightVNC, UltraVNC, Radmin, mRemote, TeamViewer, FileZilla, pcAnyware, and Remote Desktop. Another Lazarus Group malware sample checks for the presence of the following Registry key:HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Bitcoin\Bitcoin-Qt.[3][22][15]

Lazarus Group.name: Reflective Code Loading
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has changed memory protection permissions then overwritten in memory DLL function code with shellcode, which was later executed via KernelCallbackTable hijacking. Lazarus Group has also used shellcode within macros to decrypt and manually map DLLs into memory at runtime.[19][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware SierraCharlie uses RDP for propagation.[3][23]

Lazarus Group.name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware SierraAlfa accesses the ADMIN$ share via SMB to conduct lateral movement.[3][23]

Lazarus Group.name: Remote Services: SSH
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group used SSH and the PuTTy PSCP utility to gain access to a restricted segment of a compromised network.[14]

Lazarus Group.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used schtasks for persistence including through the periodic execution of a remote XSL script or a dropped VBS payload.[9][20][21]

Lazarus Group.name: Search Open Websites/Domains: Social Media
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used LinkedIn to identify and target specific employees within a chosen organization.[9][13]

Lazarus Group.name: Service Stop
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has stopped the MSExchangeIS service to render Exchange contents inaccessible to users.[10]

Lazarus Group.name: Stage Capabilities: Upload Malware
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has hosted malicious files on compromised as well as Lazarus Group-controlled servers.[13][9][26]

Lazarus Group.name: Stage Capabilities: Upload Tool
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has hosted custom and open-source tools on compromised as well as Lazarus Group-controlled servers.[9]

Lazarus Group.name: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has digitally signed malware and utilities to evade detection.[9][19]

Lazarus Group.name: System Binary Proxy Execution
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group lnk files used for persistence have abused the Windows Update Client (wuauclt.exe) to execute a malicious DLL.[19][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Mshta
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used mshta.exe to execute HTML pages downloaded by initial access documents.[19][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Regsvr32
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used rgsvr32 to execute custom malware.[9]

Lazarus Group.name: Rundll32
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used rundll32 to execute malicious payloads on a compromised host.[18][9][21]

Lazarus Group.name: System Information Discovery
Lazarus Group.Description: Several Lazarus Group malware families collect information on the type and version of the victim OS, as well as the victim computer name and CPU information. A Destover-like variant used by Lazarus Group also collects disk space information and sends it to its C2 server.[3][10][22][15][25][19]

Lazarus Group.name: System Location Discovery: System Language Discovery
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has deployed malware designed not to run on computers set to Korean, Japanese, or Chinese in Windows language preferences.[13]

Lazarus Group.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia obtains and sends to its C2 server information about the first network interface card’s configuration, including IP address, gateways, subnet mask, DHCP information, and whether WINS is available.[3][22]

Lazarus Group.name: System Network Connections Discovery
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used net use to identify and establish a network connection with a remote host.[14]

Lazarus Group.name: System Owner/User Discovery
Lazarus Group.Description: Various Lazarus Group malware enumerates logged-on users.[3][10][22][23][15][16][19]

Lazarus Group.name: System Shutdown/Reboot
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has rebooted systems after destroying files and wiping the MBR on infected systems.[24]

Lazarus Group.name: System Time Discovery
Lazarus Group.Description: A Destover-like implant used by Lazarus Group can obtain the current system time and send it to the C2 server.[25]

Lazarus Group.name: Template Injection
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used DOCX files to retrieve a malicious document template/DOTM file.[13][18]

Lazarus Group.name: User Execution: Malicious Link
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has sent spearphishing emails in an attempt to lure users to click on a malicious link.[9][13]

Lazarus Group.name: User Execution: Malicious File
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has attempted to get users to launch a malicious Microsoft Word attachment delivered via a spearphishing email.[28][13][14][19][20]

Lazarus Group.name: Valid Accounts
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used administrator credentials to gain access to restricted network segments.[14]

Lazarus Group.name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: System Checks
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used tools to detect sandbox or VMware services through identifying the presence of a debugger or related services.[13]

Lazarus Group.name: Web Service: Bidirectional Communication
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used GitHub as C2, pulling hosted image payloads then committing command execution output to files in specific directories.[19]

Lazarus Group.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used WMIC for discovery as well as to execute payloads for persistence and lateral movement.[3][23][13][14][20]

Lazarus Group.name: XSL Script Processing
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has used WMIC to execute a remote XSL script to establish persistence.[9]

Lazarus Group.name: Spearphishing Attachment
Lazarus Group.Description: Lazarus Group has been observed targeting organizations using spearphishing documents with embedded malicious payloads. [31] Highly targeted spear phishing campaigns have been conducted against a U.S. electric grid company. [32]

menuPass.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
menuPass.Description: menuPass executes commands using a command-line interface and reverse shell. The group has used a modified version of pentesting script wmiexec.vbs to execute commands.[6][11][12][10] menuPass has used malicious macros embedded inside Office documents to execute files.[9][10]

menuPass.name: Data from Local System
menuPass.Description: menuPass has collected various files from the compromised computers.[1][8]

menuPass.name: Data from Network Shared Drive
menuPass.Description: menuPass has collected data from remote systems by mounting network shares with net use and using Robocopy to transfer data.[6]

menuPass.name: Data Staged: Local Data Staging
menuPass.Description: menuPass stages data prior to exfiltration in multi-part archives, often saved in the Recycle Bin.[6]

menuPass.name: Data Staged: Remote Data Staging
menuPass.Description: menuPass has staged data on remote MSP systems or other victim networks prior to exfiltration.[6][8]

menuPass.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used certutil in a macro to decode base64-encoded content contained in a dropper document attached to an email. The group has also used certutil -decode to decode files on the victim’s machine when dropping UPPERCUT.[9][10]

menuPass.name: Dynamic Resolution: Fast Flux DNS
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used dynamic DNS service providers to host malicious domains.[2]

menuPass.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
menuPass.Description: menuPass has leveraged vulnerabilities in Pulse Secure VPNs to hijack sessions.[13]

menuPass.name: Exploitation of Remote Services
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used tools to exploit the ZeroLogon vulnerability (CVE-2020-1472).[8]

menuPass.name: File and Directory Discovery
menuPass.Description: menuPass has searched compromised systems for folders of interest including those related to HR, audit and expense, and meeting memos.[8]

menuPass.name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order Hijacking
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used DLL search order hijacking.[6]

menuPass.name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used DLL side-loading to launch versions of Mimikatz and PwDump6 as well as UPPERCUT.[11][10][8]

menuPass.name: Indicator Removal: Clear Command History
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used Wevtutil to remove PowerShell execution logs.[13]

menuPass.name: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
menuPass.Description: A menuPass macro deletes files after it has decoded and decompressed them.[9][2]

menuPass.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
menuPass.Description: menuPass has installed updates and new malware on victims.[6][2]

menuPass.name: Input Capture: Keylogging
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used key loggers to steal usernames and passwords.[2]

menuPass.name: Masquerading
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used esentutl to change file extensions to their true type that were masquerading as .txt files.[10]

menuPass.name: Rename System Utilities
menuPass.Description: menuPass has renamed certutil and moved it to a different location on the system to avoid detection based on use of the tool.[10]

menuPass.name: Match Legitimate Name or Location
menuPass.Description: menuPass has been seen changing malicious files to appear legitimate.[2]

menuPass.name: Native API
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used native APIs including GetModuleFileName, lstrcat, CreateFile, and ReadFile.[8]

menuPass.name: Network Service Discovery
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used tcping.exe, similar to Ping, to probe port status on systems of interest.[11]

menuPass.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
menuPass.Description: menuPass has encoded strings in its malware with base64 as well as with a simple, single-byte XOR obfuscation using key 0x40.[9][10][8]

menuPass.name: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used and modified open-source tools like Impacket, Mimikatz, and pwdump.[11]

menuPass.name: OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used a modified version of pentesting tools wmiexec.vbs and secretsdump.py to dump credentials.[11][12]

menuPass.name: OS Credential Dumping: NTDS
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used Ntdsutil to dump credentials.[8]

menuPass.name: OS Credential Dumping: LSA Secrets
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used a modified version of pentesting tools wmiexec.vbs and secretsdump.py to dump credentials.[11][12]

menuPass.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
menuPass.Description: menuPass has sent malicious Office documents via email as part of spearphishing campaigns as well as executables disguised as documents.[11][7][10][2]

menuPass.name: Process Injection: Process Hollowing
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used process hollowing in iexplore.exe to load the RedLeaves implant.[9]

menuPass.name: Proxy: External Proxy
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used a global service provider's IP as a proxy for C2 traffic from a victim.[7][10]

menuPass.name: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used RDP connections to move across the victim network.[6][2]

menuPass.name: Remote Services: SSH
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used Putty Secure Copy Client (PSCP) to transfer data.[6]

menuPass.name: Remote System Discovery
menuPass.Description: menuPass uses scripts to enumerate IP ranges on the victim network. menuPass has also issued the command net view /domain to a PlugX implant to gather information about remote systems on the network.[11][7]

menuPass.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used a script (atexec.py) to execute a command on a target machine via Task Scheduler.[11]

menuPass.name: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing
menuPass.Description: menuPass has resized and added data to the certificate table to enable the signing of modified files with legitimate signatures.[13]

menuPass.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: InstallUtil
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used InstallUtil.exe to execute malicious software.[11]

menuPass.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used several tools to scan for open NetBIOS nameservers and enumerate NetBIOS sessions.[11]

menuPass.name: System Network Connections Discovery
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used net use to conduct connectivity checks to machines.[6]

menuPass.name: Trusted Relationship
menuPass.Description: menuPass has used legitimate access granted to Managed Service Providers in order to access victims of interest.[11][7][8][1][2]

menuPass.name: User Execution: Malicious File
menuPass.Description: menuPass has attempted to get victims to open malicious files such as Windows Shortcuts (.lnk) and/or Microsoft Office documents, sent via email as part of spearphishing campaigns.[11][7][9][10][2]

menuPass.name: Valid Accounts

MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has used PowerShell for execution.[11][14][12][3][4][13][6][9][7][8]

MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has used a custom tool for creating reverse shells.[3]

MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has used developed tools in Python including Out1.[9]

MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has run tools including Browser64 to steal passwords saved in victim web browsers.[3][9]

MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has used tools to encode C2 communications including Base64 encoding.[5][9]

MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has stored a decoy PDF file within a victim's %temp% folder.[8]

MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has used AES to encrypt C2 responses.[8]

MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has used a Word Template, Normal.dotm, for persistence.[6]

MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has used a legitimate application, ScreenConnect, to manage systems remotely and move laterally.[9][10]

MuddyWater.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has used scheduled tasks to establish persistence.[6]

MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has used malware that leveraged rundll32.exe in a Registry Run key to execute a .dll.[12]

MuddyWater.Description: MuddyWater has used malware to collect the victim’s IP address and domain name.[12]

MuddyWater.name: System Network Connections Discovery

MuddyWater.name: System Owner/User Discovery

Rocke.Description: Rocke has executed wget and curl commands to Pastebin over the HTTPS protocol.[2]

Rocke.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
Rocke.Description: Rocke's miner has created UPX-packed files in the Windows Start Menu Folder.[1]

Rocke.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
Rocke.Description: Rocke has installed an "init.d" startup script to maintain persistence.[2]

Rocke.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell
Rocke.Description: Rocke used shell scripts to run commands which would obtain persistence and execute the cryptocurrency mining malware.[1]

Rocke.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python
Rocke.Description: Rocke has used Python-based malware to install and spread their coinminer.[2]

Rocke.name: Create or Modify System Process: Systemd Service
Rocke.Description: Rocke has installed a systemd service script to maintain persistence.[2]

Rocke.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
Rocke.Description: Rocke has extracted tar.gz files after downloading them from a C2 server.[1]

Rocke.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
Rocke.Description: Rocke exploited Apache Struts, Oracle WebLogic (CVE-2017-10271), and Adobe ColdFusion (CVE-2017-3066) vulnerabilities to deliver malware.[1][3]

Rocke.name: File and Directory Permissions Modification: Linux and Mac File and Directory Permissions Modification
Rocke.Description: Rocke has changed file permissions of files so they could not be modified.[2]

Rocke.name: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Files and Directories
Rocke.Description: Rocke downloaded a file "libprocesshider", which could hide files on the target system.[1][3]

Rocke.name: Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking
Rocke.Description: Rocke has modified /etc/ld.so.preload to hook libc functions in order to hide the installed dropper and mining software in process lists.[2]

Rocke.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
Rocke.Description: Rocke used scripts which detected and uninstalled antivirus software.[1][3]

Rocke.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall
Rocke.Description: Rocke used scripts which killed processes and added firewall rules to block traffic related to other cryptominers.[1]

Rocke.name: Indicator Removal: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs
Rocke.Description: Rocke has cleared log files within the /var/log/ folder.[2]

Rocke.name: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
Rocke.Description: Rocke has deleted files on infected machines.[2]

Rocke.name: Indicator Removal: Timestomp
Rocke.Description: Rocke has changed the time stamp of certain files.[2]

Rocke.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
Rocke.Description: Rocke used malware to download additional malicious files to the target system.[1]

Rocke.name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
Rocke.Description: Rocke has used shell scripts which download mining executables and saves them with the filename "java".[1]

Rocke.name: Network Service Discovery
Rocke.Description: Rocke conducted scanning for exposed TCP port 7001 as well as SSH and Redis servers.[1][2]

Rocke.name: Non-Standard Port
Rocke.Description: Rocke's miner connects to a C2 server using port 51640.[2]

Rocke.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
Rocke.Description: Rocke has modified UPX headers after packing files to break unpackers.[2]

Rocke.name: Software Packing
Rocke.Description: Rocke's miner has created UPX-packed files in the Windows Start Menu Folder.[1][3][2]

Rocke.name: Compile After Delivery
Rocke.Description: Rocke has compiled malware, delivered to victims as .c files, with the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC).[2]

Rocke.name: Process Discovery
Rocke.Description: Rocke can detect a running process's PID on the infected machine.[2]

Rocke.name: Process Injection: Portable Executable Injection
Rocke.Description: Rocke's miner, "TermsHost.exe", evaded defenses by injecting itself into Windows processes, including Notepad.exe.[1]

Rocke.name: Remote Services: SSH
Rocke.Description: Rocke has spread its coinminer via SSH.[2]

Rocke.name: Remote System Discovery
Rocke.Description: Rocke has looked for IP addresses in the known_hosts file on the infected system and attempted to SSH into them.[1]

Rocke.name: Resource Hijacking
Rocke.Description: Rocke has distributed cryptomining malware.[1][3]

Rocke.name: Rootkit
Rocke.Description: Rocke has modified /etc/ld.so.preload to hook libc functions in order to hide the installed dropper and mining software in process lists.[2]

Rocke.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Cron
Rocke.Description: Rocke installed a cron job that downloaded and executed files from the C2.[1][3][2]

Rocke.name: Software Discovery: Security Software Discovery
Rocke.Description: Rocke used scripts which detected and uninstalled antivirus software.[1][3]

Rocke.name: System Information Discovery
Rocke.Description: Rocke has used uname -m to collect the name and information about the infected system's kernel.[2]

Rocke.name: Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys
Rocke.Description: Rocke has used SSH private keys on the infected machine to spread its coinminer throughout a network.[2]

Rocke.name: Web Service
Rocke.Description: Rocke has used Pastebin, Gitee, and GitLab for Command and Control.[2][1]

Rocke.name: Dead Drop Resolver
Rocke.Description: Rocke has used Pastebin to check the version of beaconing malware and redirect to another Pastebin hosting updated malware.[2]

Rocke.Description: No Software table

RTM.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
RTM.Description: RTM has used Registry run keys to establish persistence for the RTM Trojan and other tools, such as a modified version of TeamViewer remote desktop software.[1][2]

RTM.name: Drive-by Compromise
RTM.Description: RTM has distributed its malware via the RIG and SUNDOWN exploit kits, as well as online advertising network Yandex.Direct.[1][3]

RTM.name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order Hijacking
RTM.Description: RTM has used search order hijacking to force TeamViewer to load a malicious DLL.[2]

RTM.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment

RTM.name: Remote Access Software
RTM.Description: RTM has used a modified version of TeamViewer and Remote Utilities for remote access.[2]

RTM.name: User Execution: Malicious File
RTM.Description: RTM has attempted to lure victims into opening e-mail attachments to execute malicious code.[2]

RTM.name: Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver
RTM.Description: RTM has used an RSS feed on Livejournal to update a list of encrypted C2 server names.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Account Discovery: Domain Account
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used a tool to query Active Directory using LDAP, discovering information about usernames listed in AD.[11]

Sandworm Team.name: Account Discovery: Email Account
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team used malware to enumerate email settings, including usernames and passwords, from the M.E.Doc application.[12]

Sandworm Team.name: Account Manipulation
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team used the sp_addlinkedsrvlogin command in MS-SQL to create a link between a created account and other servers in the network.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Domains
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has registered domain names and created URLs that are often designed to mimic or spoof legitimate websites, such as email login pages, online file sharing and storage websites, and password reset pages.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Server
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has leased servers from resellers instead of leasing infrastructure directly from hosting companies to enable its operations.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has scanned network infrastructure for vulnerabilities as part of its operational planning.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team's BCS-server tool connects to the designated C2 server via HTTP.[11]

Sandworm Team.name: Brute Force: Password Spraying
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used a script to attempt RPC authentication against a number of hosts.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used PowerShell scripts to run a credential harvesting tool in memory to evade defenses.[1][13]

Sandworm Team.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has run the xp_cmdshell command in MS-SQL.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has created VBScripts to run an SSH server.[14][11][15][13]

Sandworm Team.name: Compromise Infrastructure: Botnet
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used a large-scale botnet to target Small Office/Home Office (SOHO) network devices.[16]

Sandworm Team.name: Create Account
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team added a login to a SQL Server with sp_addlinkedsrvlogin.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: Domain Account
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has created new domain accounts on an ICS access server.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team's CredRaptor tool can collect saved passwords from various internet browsers.[11]

Sandworm Team.name: Data Destruction
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used the BlackEnergy KillDisk component to overwrite files on Windows-based Human-Machine Interfaces. [17][15]

Sandworm Team.name: Data Encoding: Standard Encoding
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team's BCS-server tool uses base64 encoding and HTML tags for the communication traffic between the C2 server.[11]

Sandworm Team.name: Data from Local System
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has exfiltrated internal documents, files, and other data from compromised hosts.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Defacement: External Defacement
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team defaced approximately 15,000 websites belonging to Georgian government, non-government, and private sector organizations in 2019.[1][2]

Sandworm Team.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team's VBS backdoor can decode Base64-encoded data and save it to the %TEMP% folder. The group also decrypted received information using the Triple DES algorithm and decompresses it using GZip.[11][12]

Sandworm Team.name: Develop Capabilities: Malware
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has developed malware for its operations, including malicious mobile applications and destructive malware such as NotPetya and Olympic Destroyer.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Disk Wipe: Disk Structure Wipe
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used the BlackEnergy KillDisk component to corrupt the infected system's master boot record.[17][15]

Sandworm Team.name: Endpoint Denial of Service
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team temporarily disrupted service to Georgian government, non-government, and private sector websites after compromising a Georgian web hosting provider in 2019.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Establish Accounts: Social Media Accounts
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has established social media accounts to disseminate victim internal-only documents and other sensitive data.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Establish Accounts: Email Accounts
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has created email accounts that mimic legitimate organizations for its spearphishing operations.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has sent system information to its C2 server using HTTP.[11]

Sandworm Team.name: Exploitation for Client Execution
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has exploited vulnerabilities in Microsoft PowerPoint via OLE objects (CVE-2014-4114) and Microsoft Word via crafted TIFF images (CVE-2013-3906).[18][19][20]

Sandworm Team.name: External Remote Services
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used Dropbear SSH with a hardcoded backdoor password to maintain persistence within the target network. Sandworm Team has also used VPN tunnels established in legitimate software company infrastructure to gain access to internal networks of that software company's users.[14][15][21]

Sandworm Team.name: File and Directory Discovery
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has enumerated files on a compromised host.[1][13]

Sandworm Team.name: Gather Victim Host Information: Software
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has researched software code to enable supply-chain operations, most notably for the 2017 NotPetya attack. Sandworm Team also collected a list of computers using specific software as part of its targeting efforts.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has obtained valid emails addresses while conducting research against target organizations that were subsequently used in spearphishing campaigns.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Employee Names
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team's research of potential victim organizations included the identification and collection of employee information.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Gather Victim Network Information: Domain Properties
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team conducted technical reconnaissance of the Parliament of Georgia's official internet domain prior to its 2019 attack.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Gather Victim Org Information: Business Relationships
Sandworm Team.Description: In preparation for its attack against the 2018 Winter Olympics, Sandworm Team conducted online research of partner organizations listed on an official PyeongChang Olympics partnership site.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has disabled event logging on compromised systems.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used backdoors that can delete files used in an attack from an infected system.[11][12]

Sandworm Team.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has pushed additional malicious tools onto an infected system to steal user credentials, move laterally, and destroy data.[11][1]

Sandworm Team.name: Input Capture: Keylogging
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used a keylogger to capture keystrokes by using the SetWindowsHookEx function.[11]

Sandworm Team.name: Lateral Tool Transfer
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used move to transfer files to a network share.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has avoided detection by naming a malicious binary explorer.exe.[11][1]

Sandworm Team.name: Network Sniffing
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used intercepter-NG to sniff passwords in network traffic.[11]

Sandworm Team.name: Non-Standard Port
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used port 6789 to accept connections on the group's SSH server.[14]

Sandworm Team.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used Base64 encoding within malware variants. Sandworm Team has also used ROT13 encoding, AES encryption and compression with the zlib library for their Python-based backdoor.[18][11]

Sandworm Team.name: Software Packing
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team used UPX to pack a copy of Mimikatz.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has acquired open-source tools for some of it's operations; for example it acquired Invoke-PSImage to establish an encrypted channel from a compromised host to Sandworm Team's C2 server as part of its preparation for the 2018 Winter Olympics attack.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Obtain Capabilities: Vulnerabilities
Sandworm Team.Description: In 2017, Sandworm Team conducted technical research related to vulnerabilities associated with websites used by the Korean Sport and Olympic Committee, a Korean power company, and a Korean airport.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team's plainpwd tool is a modified version of Mimikatz and dumps Windows credentials from system memory.[11][15]

Sandworm Team.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has delivered malicious Microsoft Office attachments via spearphishing emails.[18][17][11][1]

Sandworm Team.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has crafted phishing emails containing malicious hyperlinks.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Phishing for Information: Spearphishing Link
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has crafted spearphishing emails with hyperlinks designed to trick unwitting recipients into revealing their account credentials.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Proxy
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team's BCS-server tool can create an internal proxy server to redirect traffic from the adversary-controlled C2 to internal servers which may not be connected to the internet, but are interconnected locally.[11]

Sandworm Team.name: Remote Access Software
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used remote administration tools or remote industrial control system client software to maliciously release electricity breakers.[17]

Sandworm Team.name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has run net use to connect to network shares.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: Remote System Discovery
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used a tool to query Active Directory using LDAP, discovering information about computers listed in AD.[11][13]

Sandworm Team.name: Search Open Websites/Domains
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team researched Ukraine's unique legal entity identifier (called an "EDRPOU" number), including running queries on the EDRPOU website, in preparation for the NotPetya attack. Sandworm Team has also researched third-party websites to help it craft credible spearphishing emails.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Search Victim-Owned Websites
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has conducted research against potential victim websites as part of its operational planning.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Server Software Component: SQL Stored Procedures
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used various MS-SQL stored procedures.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: Server Software Component: Web Shell
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used webshells including P.A.S. Webshell to maintain access to victim networks.[21]

Sandworm Team.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has distributed NotPetya by compromising the legitimate Ukrainian accounting software M.E.Doc and replacing a legitimate software update with a malicious one.[22][15][1]

Sandworm Team.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team used a backdoor which could execute a supplied DLL using rundll32.exe.[12]

Sandworm Team.name: System Information Discovery
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team used a backdoor to enumerate information about the infected system's operating system.[12][1]

Sandworm Team.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team checks for connectivity to other resources in the network.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: System Network Connections Discovery
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team had gathered user, IP address, and server data related to RDP sessions on a compromised host. It has also accessed network diagram files useful for understanding how a host's network was configured.[1][13]

Sandworm Team.name: System Owner/User Discovery
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has collected the username from a compromised host.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Trusted Relationship
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used dedicated network connections from one victim organization to gain unauthorized access to a separate organization.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: User Execution: Malicious Link
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has tricked unwitting recipients into clicking on malicious hyperlinks within emails crafted to resemble trustworthy senders.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: User Execution: Malicious File
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has tricked unwitting recipients into clicking on spearphishing attachments and enabling malicious macros embedded within files.[11][1]

Sandworm Team.name: Valid Accounts
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team have used previously acquired legitimate credentials prior to attacks.[17]

Sandworm Team.name: Domain Accounts
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used stolen credentials to access administrative accounts within the domain.[1]

Sandworm Team.name: Web Service: Bidirectional Communication
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used the Telegram Bot API from Telegram Messenger to send and receive commands to its Python backdoor. Sandworm Team also used legitimate M.E.Doc software update check requests for sending and receiving commands and hosted malicious payloads on putdrive.com.[11][15]

Sandworm Team.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team has used VBScript to run WMI queries.[13]

Sandworm Team.name: Block Command Message
Sandworm Team.Description: In the Ukraine 2015 Incident, Sandworm Team blocked command messages by using malicious firmware to render communication devices inoperable. [23]

Sandworm Team.name: Block Reporting Message
Sandworm Team.Description: In the Ukraine 2015 Incident, Sandworm Team blocked reporting messages by using malicious firmware to render communication devices inoperable. [23]

Sandworm Team.name: Command-Line Interface
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team uses the MS-SQL server xp_cmdshell command, and PowerShell to execute commands. [24]

Sandworm Team.name: Connection Proxy
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team establishes an internal proxy prior to the installation of backdoors within the network. [25]

Sandworm Team.name: Device Restart/Shutdown
Sandworm Team.Description: In the 2015 attack on the Ukrainian power grid, the Sandworm Team scheduled disconnects of uninterruptable power supply (UPS) systems so that when power was disconnected from the substations, the devices would shut down and service could not be recovered. [23]

Sandworm Team.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team actors exploited vulnerabilities in GE's Cimplicity HMI and Advantech/Broadwin WebAccess HMI software which had been directly exposed to the internet. [26] [27]

Sandworm Team.name: External Remote Services
Sandworm Team.Description: In the Ukraine 2015 Incident, Sandworm Team harvested VPN worker credentials and used them to remotely log into control system networks. [23] [28] [29] [30]

Sandworm Team.name: Graphical User Interface
Sandworm Team.Description: In the Ukraine 2015 Incident, Sandworm Team utilized HMI GUIs in the SCADA environment to open breakers. [23]

Sandworm Team.name: Lateral Tool Transfer
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team used a VBS script to facilitate lateral tool transfer. The VBS script was used to copy ICS-specific payloads with the following command: cscript C:\Backinfo\ufn.vbs C:\Backinfo\101.dll C:\Delta\101.dll [24]

Sandworm Team.name: Masquerading
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team transfers executable files as .txt. and then renames them to .exe, likely to avoid detection through extension tracking. [24]

Sandworm Team.name: Remote Services
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team appears to use MS-SQL access to a pivot machine, allowing code execution throughout the ICS network. [24]

Sandworm Team.name: Scripting
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team utilized VBS and batch scripts for file movement and as wrappers for PowerShell execution. [24]

Sandworm Team.name: Spearphishing Attachment
Sandworm Team.Description: In the Ukraine 2015 incident, Sandworm Team sent spearphishing attachments to three energy distribution companies containing malware to gain access to victim systems. [31]

Sandworm Team.name: System Firmware
Sandworm Team.Description: In the Ukraine 2015 Incident, Sandworm Team developed and used malicious firmware to render communication devices inoperable. [23]

Sandworm Team.name: Unauthorized Command Message
Sandworm Team.Description: In the Ukraine 2015 Incident, Sandworm Team issued unauthorized commands to substation breakers after gaining control of operator workstations and accessing a distribution management system (DMS) client application. [23]

Sandworm Team.name: Valid Accounts
Sandworm Team.Description: Sandworm Team used valid accounts to laterally move through VPN connections and dual-homed systems. [32] [24] In the Ukraine 2015 Incident, Sandworm Team used the credentials of valid accounts to interact with client applications and access employee workstations hosting HMI applications. [23]

Tropic Trooper.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has used HTTP in communication with the C2.[5][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Application Layer Protocol: DNS
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper's backdoor has communicated to the C2 over the DNS protocol.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Automated Collection
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has collected information automatically using the adversary's USBferry attack.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Automated Exfiltration
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has used a copy function to automatically exfiltrate sensitive data from air-gapped systems using USB storage.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has created shortcuts in the Startup folder to establish persistence.[5][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Winlogon Helper DLL
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has created the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell and sets the value to establish persistence.[2][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has used Windows command scripts.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has installed a service pointing to a malicious DLL dropped to disk.[6]

Tropic Trooper.name: Data Encoding: Standard Encoding
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has used base64 encoding to hide command strings delivered from the C2.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper used shellcode with an XOR algorithm to decrypt a payload. Tropic Trooper also decrypted image files which contained a payload.[2][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Encrypted Channel
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has encrypted traffic with the C2 to prevent network detection.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Asymmetric Cryptography
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has used SSL to connect to C2 servers.[1][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium: Exfiltration over USB
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has exfiltrated data using USB storage devices.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Exploitation for Client Execution
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has executed commands through Microsoft security vulnerabilities, including CVE-2017-11882, CVE-2018-0802, and CVE-2012-0158.[1][2]

Tropic Trooper.name: File and Directory Discovery
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has monitored files' modified time.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Files and Directories
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has created a hidden directory under C:\ProgramData\Apple\Updates\ and C:\Users\Public\Documents\Flash\.[1][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has been known to side-load DLLs using a valid version of a Windows Address Book and Windows Defender executable with one of their tools.[7][5]

Tropic Trooper.name: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has deleted dropper files on an infected system using command scripts.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has used a delivered trojan to download additional files.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has hidden payloads in Flash directories and fake installer files.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Native API
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has used multiple Windows APIs including HttpInitialize, HttpCreateHttpHandle, and HttpAddUrl.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Network Service Discovery
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper used pr and an openly available tool to scan for open ports on target systems.[8][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Network Share Discovery
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper used netview to scan target systems for shared resources.[8]

Tropic Trooper.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has encrypted configuration files.[1][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Steganography
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has used JPG files with encrypted payloads to mask their backdoor routines and evade detection.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper sent spearphishing emails that contained malicious Microsoft Office and fake installer file attachments.[2][8][9][5][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Process Discovery
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper is capable of enumerating the running processes on the system using pslist.[2][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Process Injection: Dynamic-link Library Injection
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has injected a DLL backdoor into dllhost.exe and svchost.exe.[1][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Replication Through Removable Media
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has attempted to transfer USBferry from an infected USB device by copying an Autorun function to the target machine.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Server Software Component: Web Shell
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has started a web service in the target host and wait for the adversary to connect, acting as a web shell.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Software Discovery
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper's backdoor could list the infected system's installed software.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: Security Software Discovery
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper can search for anti-virus software running on the system.[2]

Tropic Trooper.name: System Information Discovery
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has detected a target system’s OS version and system volume information.[8][3]

Tropic Trooper.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has used scripts to collect the host's network topology.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: System Network Connections Discovery
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has tested if the localhost network is available and other connection capability on an infected system using command scripts.[3]

Tropic Trooper.name: System Owner/User Discovery
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper used letmein to scan for saved usernames on the target system.[8]

Tropic Trooper.name: Template Injection
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper delivered malicious documents with the XLSX extension, typically used by OpenXML documents, but the file itself was actually an OLE (XLS) document.[2]

Tropic Trooper.name: User Execution: Malicious File
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has lured victims into executing malware via malicious e-mail attachments.[5]

Tropic Trooper.name: Valid Accounts: Local Accounts
Tropic Trooper.Description: Tropic Trooper has used known administrator account credentials to execute the backdoor directly.[3]
