Turla.name: Access Token Manipulation: Create Process with Token
Turla.Description: Turla RPC backdoors can impersonate or steal process tokens before executing commands.[11]

Turla.name: Account Discovery: Local Account
Turla.Description: Turla has used net user to enumerate local accounts on the system.[12][13]

Turla.name: Account Discovery: Domain Account
Turla.Description: Turla has used net user /domain to enumerate domain accounts.[12]

Turla.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Web Services
Turla.Description: Turla has created web accounts including Dropbox and GitHub for C2 and document exfiltration.[13]

Turla.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
Turla.Description: Turla has used HTTP and HTTPS for C2 communications.[4][14]

Turla.name: Application Layer Protocol: Mail Protocols
Turla.Description: Turla has used multiple backdoors which communicate with a C2 server via email attachments.[15]

Turla.name: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility
Turla.Description: Turla has encrypted files stolen from connected USB drives into a RAR file before exfiltration.[16]

Turla.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
Turla.Description: A Turla Javascript backdoor added a local_update_check value under the Registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run to establish persistence. Additionally, a Turla custom executable containing Metasploit shellcode is saved to the Startup folder to gain persistence.[4][14]

Turla.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Winlogon Helper DLL
Turla.Description: Turla established persistence by adding a Shell value under the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon.[4]

Turla.name: Brute Force
Turla.Description: Turla may attempt to connect to systems within a victim's network using net use commands and a predefined list or collection of passwords.[1]

Turla.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
Turla.Description: Turla has used PowerShell to execute commands/scripts, in some cases via a custom executable or code from Empire's PSInject.[14][11][16] Turla has also used PowerShell scripts to load and execute malware in memory.

Turla.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
Turla.Description: Turla RPC backdoors have used cmd.exe to execute commands.[11][16]

Turla.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
Turla.Description: Turla has used VBS scripts throughout its operations.[16]

Turla.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python
Turla.Description: Turla has used IronPython scripts as part of the IronNetInjector toolchain to drop payloads.[17]

Turla.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript
Turla.Description: Turla has used various JavaScript-based backdoors.[4]

Turla.name: Compromise Infrastructure: Virtual Private Server
Turla.Description: Turla has used the VPS infrastructure of compromised Iranian threat actors.[18]

Turla.name: Compromise Infrastructure: Server
Turla.Description: Turla has used compromised servers as infrastructure.[19][7][10]

Turla.name: Compromise Infrastructure: Web Services
Turla.Description: Turla has frequently used compromised WordPress sites for C2 infrastructure.[19]

Turla.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager
Turla.Description: Turla has gathered credentials from the Windows Credential Manager tool.[16]

Turla.name: Data from Information Repositories
Turla.Description: Turla has used a custom .NET tool to collect documents from an organization's internal central database.[12]

Turla.name: Data from Local System
Turla.Description: Turla RPC backdoors can upload files from victim machines.[11]

Turla.name: Data from Removable Media
Turla.Description: Turla RPC backdoors can collect files from USB thumb drives.[11][16]

Turla.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
Turla.Description: Turla has used a custom decryption routine, which pulls key and salt values from other artifacts such as a WMI filter or PowerShell Profile, to decode encrypted PowerShell payloads.[11]

Turla.name: Develop Capabilities: Malware
Turla.Description: Turla has developed its own unique malware for use in operations.[19]

Turla.name: Drive-by Compromise
Turla.Description: Turla has infected victims using watering holes.[12][5]

Turla.name: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription
Turla.Description: Turla has used WMI event filters and consumers to establish persistence.[11]

Turla.name: Event Triggered Execution: PowerShell Profile
Turla.Description: Turla has used PowerShell profiles to maintain persistence on an infected machine.[11]

Turla.name: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
Turla.Description: Turla has used WebDAV to upload stolen USB files to a cloud drive.[16] Turla has also exfiltrated stolen files to OneDrive and 4shared.[12]

Turla.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
Turla.Description: Turla has exploited vulnerabilities in the VBoxDrv.sys driver to obtain kernel mode privileges.[20]

Turla.name: File and Directory Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover files in specific locations on the hard disk %TEMP% directory, the current user's desktop, the Program Files directory, and Recent.[1][12] Turla RPC backdoors have also searched for files matching the lPH*.dll pattern.[11]

Turla.name: Group Policy Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover Group Policy details using the gpresult command.[12]

Turla.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
Turla.Description: Turla has used a AMSI bypass, which patches the in-memory amsi.dll, in PowerShell scripts to bypass Windows antimalware products.[11]

Turla.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
Turla.Description: Turla has used shellcode to download Meterpreter after compromising a victim.[14]

Turla.name: Lateral Tool Transfer
Turla.Description: Turla RPC backdoors can be used to transfer files to/from victim machines on the local network.[11][16]

Turla.name: Modify Registry
Turla.Description: Turla has used the Registry to store encrypted payloads.[11][16]

Turla.name: Native API
Turla.Description: Turla and its RPC backdoors have used APIs calls for various tasks related to subverting AMSI and accessing then executing commands through RPC and/or named pipes.[11]

Turla.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
Turla.Description: Turla has used encryption (including salted 3DES via PowerSploit's Out-EncryptedScript.ps1), random variable names, and base64 encoding to obfuscate PowerShell commands and payloads.[11]

Turla.name: Indicator Removal from Tools
Turla.Description: Based on comparison of Gazer versions, Turla made an effort to obfuscate strings in the malware that could be used as IoCs, including the mutex name and named pipe.[2]

Turla.name: Obtain Capabilities: Malware
Turla.Description: Turla has used malware obtained after compromising other threat actors, such as OilRig.[18][19]

Turla.name: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
Turla.Description: Turla has obtained and customized publicly-available tools like Mimikatz.[16]

Turla.name: Password Policy Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla has used net accounts and net accounts /domain to acquire password policy information.[12]

Turla.name: Peripheral Device Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla has used fsutil fsinfo drives to list connected drives.[12]

Turla.name: Permission Groups Discovery: Local Groups
Turla.Description: Turla has used net localgroup and net localgroup Administrators to enumerate group information, including members of the local administrators group.[12]

Turla.name: Permission Groups Discovery: Domain Groups
Turla.Description: Turla has used net group "Domain Admins" /domain to identify domain administrators.[12]

Turla.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
Turla.Description: Turla attempted to trick targets into clicking on a link featuring a seemingly legitimate domain from Adobe.com to download their malware and gain initial access.[4]

Turla.name: Process Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover running processes using the tasklist /v command.[1] Turla RPC backdoors have also enumerated processes associated with specific open ports or named pipes.[11]

Turla.name: Process Injection
Turla.Description: Turla has also used PowerSploit's Invoke-ReflectivePEInjection.ps1 to reflectively load a PowerShell payload into a random process on the victim system.[11]

Turla.name: Dynamic-link Library Injection
Turla.Description: Turla has used Metasploit to perform reflective DLL injection in order to escalate privileges.[14][21]

Turla.name: Proxy
Turla.Description: Turla RPC backdoors have included local UPnP RPC proxies.[11]

Turla.name: Internal Proxy
Turla.Description: Turla has compromised internal network systems to act as a proxy to forward traffic to C2.[10]

Turla.name: Query Registry
Turla.Description: Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover information in the Windows Registry with the reg query command.[1] Turla has also retrieved PowerShell payloads hidden in Registry keys as well as checking keys associated with null session named pipes .[11]

Turla.name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
Turla.Description: Turla used net use commands to connect to lateral systems within a network.[1]

Turla.name: Remote System Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover remote systems on a local network using the net view and net view /DOMAIN commands. Turla has also used net group "Domain Computers" /domain, net group "Domain Controllers" /domain, and net group "Exchange Servers" /domain to enumerate domain computers, including the organization's DC and Exchange Server.[1][12]

Turla.name: Software Discovery: Security Software Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla has obtained information on security software, including security logging information that may indicate whether their malware has been detected.[12]

Turla.name: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing Policy Modification
Turla.Description: Turla has modified variables in kernel memory to turn off Driver Signature Enforcement after exploiting vulnerabilities that obtained kernel mode privileges.[20][22]

Turla.name: System Information Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover operating system configuration details using the systeminfo and set commands.[1][12]

Turla.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover network configuration details using the arp -a, nbtstat -n, net config, ipconfig /all, and route commands, as well as NBTscan.[1][16][12] Turla RPC backdoors have also retrieved registered RPC interface information from process memory.[11]

Turla.name: Internet Connection Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla has used tracert to check internet connectivity.[12]

Turla.name: System Network Connections Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover active local network connections using the netstat -an, net use, net file, and net session commands.[1][12] Turla RPC backdoors have also enumerated the IPv4 TCP connection table via the GetTcpTable2 API call.[11]

Turla.name: System Service Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover running services and associated processes using the tasklist /svc command.[1]

Turla.name: System Time Discovery
Turla.Description: Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover the system time by using the net time command.[1]

Turla.name: User Execution: Malicious Link
Turla.Description: Turla has used spearphishing via a link to get users to download and run their malware.[4]

Turla.name: Valid Accounts: Local Accounts
Turla.Description: Turla has abused local accounts that have the same password across the victim’s network.[13]

Turla.name: Web Service
Turla.Description: Turla has used legitimate web services including Pastebin, Dropbox, and GitHub for C2 communications.[7][13]

Turla.name: Bidirectional Communication
Turla.Description: A Turla JavaScript backdoor has used Google Apps Script as its C2 server.[4][14]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Domains
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has purchased domains for use in targeted campaigns.[1]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Web Services
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used GitHub to host malware linked in spearphishing e-mails.[3][4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has created a Registry Run key named Dropbox Update Setup to establish persistence for a malicious Python binary.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to open a Windows Command Shell on a remote host.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used Python-based implants to interact with compromised hosts.[3][4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to steal credentials from installed web browsers including Microsoft Internet Explorer and Google Chrome.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used the AES256 algorithm with a SHA1 derived key to decrypt exploit code.[2]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used AES encrypted communications in C2.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has exfiltrated files via the Dropbox API C2.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has exfiltrated stolen data to Dropbox.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has exploited CVE-2017-0005 for local privilege escalation.[2]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used tools to download malicious files to compromised hosts.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Masquerading
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has spoofed legitimate applications in phishing lures and changed file extensions to conceal installation of malware.[3][4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Masquerade Task or Service
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has created a run key named Dropbox Update Setup to mask a persistence mechanism for a malicious binary.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used multi-stage packers for exploit code.[2]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used malicious links and web beacons in e-mails for malware download and to track hits to attacker-controlled URL's.[1][3][4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Phishing for Information
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM targeted presidential campaign staffers with credential phishing e-mails.[3]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Query Registry
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to query the Registry for proxy settings.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Msiexec
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used the msiexec.exe command-line utility to download and execute malicious MSI files.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: System Information Discovery
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to capture the processor architecture of a compromised host in order to register it with C2.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to enumerate proxy settings in the target environment.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: System Owner/User Discovery
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to capture the username on a compromised host in order to register it with C2.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: System Time Discovery
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to capture the time on a compromised host in order to register it with C2.[4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: User Execution: Malicious Link
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used malicious links in e-mails to lure victims into downloading malware.[3][4]

ZIRCONIUM.name: Web Service: Bidirectional Communication
ZIRCONIUM.Description: ZIRCONIUM has used Dropbox for C2 allowing upload and download of files as well as execution of arbitrary commands.[3][4]
